World.title: How India's blocking of a film exposing real-life police abuses backfired
World.content:
How India's blocking of a film exposing real-life police abuses backfired

toggle caption Omkar Khandekar/NPR

AMRITSAR, India — On a muggy monsoon evening, farmers in the northern Indian village of Bandala finished tending to their rice and sugarcane crop and flocked to the local Sikh temple. They settled in plastic chairs, women to the front, men to the back, as volunteers served strawberry juice in plastic cups and kids bustled around, happy to have an excuse to stay up late.

They were gathered for an unlikely event: the screening of a film that was never granted a theatrical release certificate by Indian censors, and pulled from a streaming platform a day after its release online. The Indian government has not revealed its reasons for the blocking. India's Ministry of Information and Broadcasting did not reply to NPR's interview requests.

Sponsor Message

There was little sign of the film's contraband nature in the promotional posters plastered all over the village shopfronts and playground walls. They advertised the movie, titled Satluj, as based on real-life events that addressed the history and identity of Sikhs, a religious minority within India numbering more than 20 million people and forming a majority in the northern state of Punjab.

toggle caption Narinder Nanu/AFP via Getty Images

Satluj is a biopic of Jaswant Singh Khalra, an activist who was killed after uncovering extrajudicial killings carried out by security forces, primarily the Punjab police. This occurred after the separatist movement turned violent in 1984, when the Indian army stormed and damaged the Golden Temple, one of the holiest shrines for Sikhs, during a gunfight with militants that had sought refuge there. The following decade witnessed several killings of civilians, militants and state officials, including the assassination of former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi by her Sikh bodyguard.

Ordinarily, Satluj would have joined the long list of films that the Indian government has blocked, or forced directors to tone down in recent years. But the ostensible banning of Satluj triggered something else: rare defiance against the Hindu nationalist government of Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

In cities and villages across Punjab, Sikh leaders urged their community to watch it. In its spiritual capital Amritsar, activists and political parties staged rallies opposing the ban. Many organized screenings in Sikh temple courtyards and public streets. Others downloaded bootleg copies and shared them on WhatsApp and YouTube.

Sponsor Message

Such pushback against the state's diktats is quite unusual, says Sanjay Srivastava, a sociologist at SOAS University of London. "It does reflect a genuine feeling on the ground that the issues covered in the film have not been entirely resolved," he says.

The militant movement for a Sikh state

toggle caption Omkar Khandekar/NPR

Satluj is set during the '90s, a few years after a Sikh separatist movement had turned militant. Thousands of Sikhs died in clashes and gunfights with Indian security forces. Many fled to countries like the U.S. and Canada and sought asylum.

Sarabjit Singh Verka, a lawyer with the nonprofit Punjab Human Rights Organisation in Amritsar, has represented many victims of the violence. He says Indian authorities back then were desperate to end the violence. "Some police officers on trial confessed to me in private that they were allowed to kill militants who had killed two or more people," says Verka. "The police called the policy 'bullet for bullet'."

This carte blanche, Verka says, started because civilians were often too scared to testify against militants in the court, which allowed many to go free. "But some officers turned this into an extortion racket. They would kidnap young men and demand ransom from their families. Some also staged shootouts and cremated bodies to cover up the evidence."

Amid this violence in the 1990s, Amritsar resident Jaswant Singh Khalra quit his job at a local bank to document such killings. In Satluj, one of India's top stars, Diljit Dosanjh, plays his role.

Using municipal and crematorium records, Khalra compiled a list of around 2,000 youths that he claimed the police had killed in his home district of Amritsar. He then approached the Punjab High Court and the Supreme Court, claiming the toll across the state of Punjab could be up to 25,000.

Human rights lawyer Verka says that number is likely an exaggeration. "The government should've nevertheless set up a truth and reconciliation commission to ascertain the truth. They didn't."

Sponsor Message

In 1995, a few months after he made the allegations, Khalra disappeared from his home. His body was never found. A decade later, an Indian trial court convicted six police officers for his abduction and murder. "And while the government compensated some victims, most perpetrators got away," adds Verka.

He says Indian authorities didn't want to answer for state excesses then — and they don't appear to want it now.

The pushback against censorship

toggle caption Prabhjot Gill/AP

The filmmakers of Satluj say they were ready to release it in cinema halls by December 2022. In an interview with NPR, director Honey Trehan recalled that officials on India's film certification board stalled them for nearly four years. Trehan recalled arguing with a board official that the film was based on news reports and court testimonies: "He looked at me and said, 'Who speaks the truth so loudly in today's times?'"

Filmmakers don't need an official certificate to put up their works online. But two days after releasing the film in July, the streaming platform Zee5 took it down with a cryptic Instagram post blaming "current developments." As people started screening bootleg copies, the service said it was "doing everything" to bring the film back. The film remains unavailable on the platform.

Jagmohan Singh Raju, general secretary of the ruling BJP in Punjab, says authorities were concerned that the film's portrayal of police violence could revive sentiments of Sikh separatism, a threat New Delhi views with heightened urgency following escalating tensions with overseas Sikh diaspora communities.

In recent years, India's Hindu nationalist government has repeatedly criticized countries like Canada and the United Kingdom for harboring Sikh separatists. In 2024, the United States charged an Indian intelligence agent for conspiring to kill one such separatist, Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, in New York. Canadian authorities also charged four Indian nationals linked to jailed Indian gangster Lawrence Bishnoi's network with the 2023 murder of separatist Hardeep Singh Nijjar.

Sponsor Message

Analysts say fearing that international activism could reignite unrest at home, Indian authorities treat historical narratives like Satluj not just as movies, but as potential security risks.

Still, the BJP official Raju acknowledged that one film wouldn't immediately radicalize an audience. "It doesn't happen overnight that a crowd will gather and they become separatists," he said. But it would trigger that kind of thinking. "This first seeps into your mind, gets into your psychology, then someone plays on that psychology. It's a long game."

Film journalist Anna M.M. Vetticad says the way the Hindu nationalist government reacted to Satluj follows their understanding of the power of cinema. "This government clearly considers cinema as a way of influencing mindsets, as a means of propaganda," she says. "You can see that from the spate of Hindi cinema that is completely Islamophobic, pro-BJP and doing PR for this government."

She adds that the idea that the movie would trigger separatist feelings missed the point of Satluj. "It is focusing on human rights violations by those in authority. And when an individual investigated it, he was murdered for doing so."

Preserving memory

toggle caption Omkar Khandekar/NPR

For the audience who watched Satluj at Bandala and other villages, the public screenings were about something else.

In 1990, Ranjit Singh Babbar was 3 years old when police from Punjab's Kapurthala district detained his farmer father, Sardar Atma Singh. Babbar claims his father had no association with the militants, yet the police demanded an equivalent of $12,000 to release him. "My family sold land, gold and put it together. But when they returned with the ransom, the police said it was too late."

toggle caption Omkar Khandekar/NPR

Babbar shows a passport-size photo he carries in his wallet of a young man with a lush beard, wearing a gray turban. "That's the only memory of my father today," he says. "The government never issued his death certificate. We couldn't even do his funeral rites. Police killed him and threw his body into a river."

Sponsor Message

Babbar says Jaswant Singh Khalra's fight for justice represented hope in India's democracy. "The blocking of his biopic sends the opposite signal," he says. "It makes us Sikhs feel like second-class citizens."

World.title: Trump says he's brokered a 'very good deal' with Canada after pausing 50% tariffs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada and U.S. negotiators are working on the final text of an agreement that would avert new tariffs and smooth over longstanding bilateral trade irritants, officials from both countries said on Wednesday.

U.S. President Donald Trump said he has brokered what he called "a very good deal" with Canada that will work out favourably for both countries, while giving few details on what exactly has been negotiated.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, meanwhile, said in his own statement on social media there had been "significant progress" with the Americans, and framed the prospective deal as one that will position Canada well compared to other countries also grappling with Trump's protectionist policies.

"Canada entered these discussions with the best overall trade terms. We are now moving towards an agreement that reinforces that Canadian advantage, including by securing the best terms in each of Canada's most important strategic sectors and providing greater certainty about our future trading relationship," Carney said.

Carney will convene a meeting of his cabinet on Wednesday afternoon to discuss the deal, according to his official itinerary. Then, Carney and his negotiators will brief the premiers on what's to come.

WATCH | Trump says deal is good for U.S. farmers: Trump claims certain Canadian tariffs on U.S. goods will be 'non-existent' | Duration 1:26 U.S. President Donald Trump says Canada and the U.S. have reached a 'very fair deal' for both countries, after pausing threatened 50 per cent tariffs on a broad range of Canadian goods. Trump says tariffs on U.S. farm goods are 'going to be eviscerated down to zero,' when the deal is finalized.

Trump paused his planned 50 per cent tariffs on nearly $30 billion worth of Canadian goods late Tuesday to allow the deal to be finalized.

A Canadian source with direct knowledge of the talks told CBC News that Ottawa was able to get tariffs on some hard-hit sectors reduced in the agreement.

Canada has been demanding relief for the steel, aluminum, auto and lumber sectors weighed down by 25 per cent or higher levies on their goods for more than a year. As previously reported, the U.S. has offered to lower those rates as part of these negotiations, but just how low has been a point of contention.

Trump said that farmers and manufacturers in particular are going to be "thrilled" with what he's agreed to do with Canada.

He said unspecified Canadian tariffs "are going to be totally eviscerated, down to zero."

The vast majority of U.S. products already trade into Canada tariff-free, but Ottawa has levied some retaliatory tariffs on U.S. autos, steel and aluminum imports since the outset of the trade war.

WATCH | Trump pauses tariffs: Trump pauses 50% tariffs, saying new trade deal reached | Duration 6:27 U.S. President Donald Trump has paused 50 per cent tariffs on Canada, saying the two countries have reached a new trade deal that just needs to be finalized. In a statement, Prime Minister Mark Carney said 'substantial progress has been made.'

Canada also has tariffs on some dairy imports that exceed a set quota. But American producers do not export enough dairy to meet Canadian tariff rate quota thresholds.

Still, Trump said what's been negotiated is "great for our farmers."

"Our farmers will no longer be held up, because they were being hurt very badly by Canada," Trump said.

Trump said the U.S. has agreed to readjust its tariff rates on Canadian autos but didn't specify by how much.

The current headline tariff rate is 25 per cent on Canadian automobile imports, a levy that caused significant economic dislocation, plant closures and lost jobs, particularly in Ontario, Canada's industrial heartland.

"They were paying a high number, we're reducing it a little bit," Trump said of auto tariffs. "You gotta give something."

While there are outlines of an agreement, Trump said that it's "still subject to finalization of documents."

Carney sees 'significant progress'

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc met with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in Washington on Wednesday morning for more talks.

Speaking briefly to reporters on his way out of the roughly 30-minute long discussion, LeBlanc answered a question about whether Canada's supply-managed dairy sector, long targeted by U.S. negotiators, will be affected by the terms of this prospective agreement.

WATCH | Canadian, U.S. negotiators answer questions: Greer and LeBlanc speak to reporters as trade talks continue | Duration 1:16 Speaking to reporters after a meeting in Washington, United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Canada and the U.S. have 'eliminated some of the irritants we've had over the past year.' Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc said he is 'very confident' in discussions about the dairy sector.

"The prime minister was very clear, we need to protect supply management. We need to ensure that the supply management regime remains entirely intact and I'm confident that that's the case," LeBlanc said.

A spokesperson for LeBlanc said the minister is headed back to Ottawa to meet with Carney "and take other meetings necessary to finalize trade negotiations."

Greer framed the forthcoming deal as a win-win.

"We've reached an agreement that will not only continue to protect American workers, American jobs, American supply chains, but really strengthen the North American economy and create a situation where North America will continue to be an energy powerhouse, a manufacturing powerhouse," he told reporters gathered outside his office.

Few details

The details of what exactly has been brokered are scant.

Neither side released any documents stating what each country could give up in return for some concessions.

Beyond Greer's assertion that there will be changes to some Canadian policies, Trump alluded to a possible revival of the Keystone XL pipeline, a long-defunct project that could carry oil from Alberta to the U.S. Gulf Coast. Trump already signed an executive order in April authorizing the construction of a similar cross-border pipeline.

WATCH | Trump's order revives parts of pipeline: Trump signs order to revive parts of cancelled Keystone XL pipeline | Duration 1:49 U.S. President ‌Donald Trump has signed an order authorizing a proposed project to transport Canadian oil across the border as part of an effort to revive parts of the cancelled Keystone XL pipeline. South Bow, the Canadian company behind Keystone XL, is partnering with U.S. company Bridger Pipeline on the proposed project.

The Americans have long demanded U.S. liquor be put back on the shelves of provincially run stores, ending a boycott that has been devastatingly effective. The Trump administration is also pushing for Canada to remove its retaliatory tariffs on U.S. autos and to change how the supply-managed dairy sector allocates quotas.

LeBlanc, meanwhile, has pushed for the U.S. to scrap the threatened 50 per cent levies, called the Section 338 tariffs. He also wants the country to lower the existing Section 232 fees on industrial products like steel, aluminum, autos and lumber.

Carney said his government is working on a deal that will "address outstanding trade issues and deliver greater certainty and real benefits for Canadian businesses, workers, farmers and families."

The business sector welcomed Trump's tariff pause and urged the two sides to get a broader deal done quickly.

Candace Laing, president and chief executive officer of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, said in a statement that "an extension doesn't bring the certainty that a signed interim deal would."

"We know that stability is in short supply and businesses will take any ounce they can get. This limbo state is not anyone's preferred outcome — time is of the essence," she said.

World.title: Key dates in Keystone XL pipeline as Trump claims contentious project being revived
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump has claimed a contentious oil pipeline project is being revived as Canada and the United States continue negotiations aimed at staving off a new batch of U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods.

Trump wrote on his Truth Social website late on Tuesday that, "The great Keystone XL Pipeline, long ago killed by Sleepy Joe Biden, may be awoken from the grave!"

The U.S. president also shared an AI-generated image showing him lifting a massive pipeline tagged "KEYSTONE" out of a grave, with two American flags waving in the background and a headstone that reads, "Buried by Biden."

Canada has not commented publicly on Trump's claim that the project is being revived as part of ongoing trade talks. Washington said late on Tuesday that it was pausing planned 50 per cent tariffs on a range of Canadian goods for three days to allow for more negotiations.

Here's a look at some key dates in the history of the Keystone XL expansion.

WATCH | Trump seeks to revive parts of Keystone XL project: Trump signs order to revive parts of cancelled Keystone XL pipeline | Duration 1:49 U.S. President ‌Donald Trump has signed an order authorizing a proposed project to transport Canadian oil across the border as part of an effort to revive parts of the cancelled Keystone XL pipeline. South Bow, the Canadian company behind Keystone XL, is partnering with U.S. company Bridger Pipeline on the proposed project.

Initial proposal, and opposition grows

July 2008: Keystone XL was first proposed back when Stephen Harper was prime minister and U.S. President George W. Bush was finishing his second term. TransCanada — now called TC Energy — and ConocoPhillips, joint owners of the Keystone pipeline, pitched a major extension to the network. The expansion, dubbed Keystone XL, would carry hundreds of thousands of barrels of oilsands bitumen from Alberta to Texas.

March 2010: The National Energy Board approves TransCanada's application for Keystone XL, though the OK comes with 22 conditions regarding safety, environmental protection and landowner rights.

Aug. 26, 2011: After an extended review, the State Department releases its final environmental assessment, which echoes an earlier draft statement in saying the pipeline would have a limited environmental impact.

August—September 2011: Protesters stage a two-week campaign of civil disobedience at the White House as wider opposition to Keystone XL grows, particularly among environmental and Indigenous groups.

The project drew protests outside the White House, including this one on Aug. 22, 2011. (J. Scott Applewhite/The Associated Press)

Obama rejects pipeline route

November 2011: The U.S. State Department says TransCanada must reroute Keystone XL to avoid an ecologically sensitive region of Nebraska. Days later, TransCanada agrees to reroute the line.

January 2012: U.S. President Barack Obama rejects Keystone, saying a timeline imposed by U.S. legislators did not leave enough time to review the new route. Obama says TransCanada is free to submit another application.

April-May 2012: TransCanada submits a new route to officials in Nebraska for approval. The company also files a new application with the State Department for the northern part of Keystone XL.

January 2013: Nebraska Gov. Dave Heineman approves TransCanada's proposed new route, sending the project back to the State Department for review. Pipeline opponents file a lawsuit against the Nebraska government claiming the state law used to review the new route is unconstitutional.

A wooden stick marks the proposed route of the Keystone XL pipeline near Bradshaw, Neb., on March 11, 2013. (Nati Harnik/The Associated Press)

April 18, 2014: The State Department suspends the regulatory process indefinitely, citing uncertainty about the court case in Nebraska.

Jan. 9, 2015: The Nebraska Supreme Court throws out the legal challenge against the project.

January-February 2015: The U.S. Senate approves a bill to build Keystone XL. Less than a month later, Obama vetoes the measure.

Nov. 6, 2015: The Obama administration rejects TransCanada's application to build Keystone XL.

Trump promises Keystone XL

Nov. 8, 2016: Donald Trump wins the U.S. presidential election after promising several times on the campaign trail that he would approve Keystone XL if elected.

Jan. 24, 2017: Trump signs an executive order that he says approves Keystone XL, but suggests the U.S. intends to renegotiate the terms of the project.

Trump signed the Keystone XL pipeline executive order on Jan. 24, 2017. (Evan Vucci/The Associated Press)

Nov. 9, 2018: A U.S. federal judge blocks the pipeline's construction to allow more time to study the potential environmental impact.

March 29, 2019: Trump issues a new presidential permit in an effort to speed up development.

May 3, 2019: TransCanada changes its name to TC Energy.

March 31, 2020: Alberta agrees to invest $1.5 billion in Keystone XL, followed by a $6 billion loan guarantee in 2021.

April 7, 2020: Construction begins, despite calls from Indigenous groups and environmentalists to pause their efforts.

Nov. 3, 2020: Joe Biden defeats Trump in the U.S. presidential election.

Biden revokes permit

Jan. 20, 2021: Biden signs an executive order on his first day in office revoking the 2019 permit Trump issued for Keystone XL, which he says is not in the U.S. national interest. Prime Minister Justin Trudeau says his government is "disappointed" by the decision.

Pipeline used to carry crude oil is shown at the Superior, Wis., terminal of Enbridge Energy. (Jim Mone/The Associated Press)

June 9, 2021: TC Energy says it has terminated the Keystone XL project "after a comprehensive review of its options, and in consultation with its partner, the Government of Alberta."

July 2021: TC Energy announces plans to file a claim under the Canada-U.S.-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) to recoup $15 billion US in damages it says were caused by the cancellation of the project. The company argues Washington breached its obligations under CUSMA's predecessor, NAFTA.

Feb. 9, 2022: The Alberta government files a notice of intent to initiate its own "legacy NAFTA claim" under CUSMA over the U.S. permit's revocation. Alberta says it wants to recover its investment in the project.

December 2022: Nearly 130,000 barrels of oil leaks from a ruptured stretch of the existing Keystone pipeline in Kansas. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) says it's "one of the largest inland oil spills in recent history."

October 2024: South Bow spins off from TC Energy ⁠to take over its oil pipeline business.

July 2024: The International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes, an international tribunal, throws out TC Energy's claim for $15 billion US in damages against the U.S. government, citing a jurisdictional issue.

Trump 2.0

February 2025: Trump, who took office for a second term in January 2025, says the company behind Keystone XL should "get it built – NOW!" in a post on his Truth Social platform. A spokesperson for South Bow says the company has "moved on from the Keystone XL project" but will "continue to engage with customers to develop options to increase Canadian oil supplies to meet growing demand."

October 2025: Prime Minister Mark Carney tells Trump during a meeting at the White House that there's renewed national interest from Canada in the Keystone XL pipeline, a source with knowledge of the discussions tells CBC.

April 30, 2026: Trump signs an order authorizing a proposed project to transport Canadian oil across the border as part of an effort to revive parts of the Keystone XL pipeline. South Bow is partnering with U.S. company Bridger Pipeline on the proposal.

WATCH | Trump approves partial revival of Keystone XL: Trump approval partly resurrects Keystone XL pipeline | Duration 2:03 U.S. President Donald Trump's order authorizing a Canada-Wyoming crude oil pipeline revives parts of the cancelled Keystone XL project. The Bridger pipeline would transport crude from Canada to the U.S. border along part of the old Keystone route.

May 2026: South Bow says it will decide by mid-2027 whether to proceed with the proposed project. The 550,000-barrel-per-day Alberta-to-Wyoming pipeline, dubbed Prairie Connector, would not follow the same U.S. route as the project cancelled in 2021 but it would use some of the already-assembled Keystone XL pipe on the Canadian side of the border.

July 2026: The U.S. government says it reached a settlement with South Bow over the 2022 oil spill in Kansas, with the company agreeing to pay more than $26 million US in civil penalties. South Bow will also pay approximately $40 million US to prevent future spills and $3 million US to help Kansas conduct natural resource restoration projects, the government says.

Aug. 18, 2026: Trump says the Keystone XL project "may be awoken from the grave!" as he agrees to postpone new 50 per cent tariffs on a range of Canadian goods by three days. In his own statement about the postponed U.S. tariffs, Carney does not mention Keystone XL.

World.title: Céline Dion reveals more about her health, treating stiff person syndrome, in new interview
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As Céline Dion prepares for her five-week residency in Paris to begin next month, she's revealing more details about her illness and what she's been doing to treat it.

The Canadian superstar disclosed in an exclusive Harper's Bazaar profile that she had symptoms of stiff person syndrome for 17 years before she was formally diagnosed in 2022 with the rare neurological autoimmune disorder.

The pain, which began flaring up in 2020, was so severe that some days she could barely walk, she told the magazine. At times, she needed a high dose of Valium to function.

Stiff person syndrome is a progressive disorder that generally gets worse over time. It affects one or two people out of every million. Symptoms can include rigid muscles and painful spasms, triggered by stress, loud noises or sudden movement. There is no clear cause, and no regulator-approved treatment specifically for the condition, though other therapies can help manage it.

Before her diagnosis, when she had to cancel a show, she'd offer a reason that concealed the true extent of her pain — often blaming a cough or sinus infection.

Dion told Harper's she could feel that something more serious was going on. She said this made her feel like she was lying to her fans, the very people whose support allowed her to later pursue extensive treatment.

"They paid for tickets,” she told the magazine. "They bought my records. They gave me that luxury."

Following her diagnosis, Dion cancelled all her remaining shows. She has not performed publicly since the Paris 2024 Olympic Games, but she is planning to return to the stage in September.

Dion's intense recovery regimen

Dion has reportedly been following an intense recovery regimen that includes medication, physical therapy, vocal therapy and immunotherapy.

The magazine also said she is doing 90-minute Pilates sessions three times a week, plus ballet classes twice a week, to prepare for her upcoming shows.

WATCH | Céline Dion vows to sing again in interview with Adrienne Arsenault: Céline Dion: I Will Sing Again | Duration 44:10 In this intensely personal, candid and revealing exclusive from the team at The National, Céline Dion opens up to CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault about coping with stiff person syndrome, losing the voice that has guided her life and how she is determined to perform again. [I Am: Celine Dion, the documentary featured in this interview, premieres June 25 on Prime Video.]

In the Harper's story, reporter Jazmine Hughes described the singer as being constantly in motion— almost afraid to sit still for too long, in case she freezes up again.

Dion considers her recovery and the ability to perform again a miracle that she said she isn't taking for granted.

"If you don’t want to sign autographs and you don’t want to get yourself pretty and you don’t want to be disturbed because your pasta is going to get cold, you can always stay home," she said. "But look at what you have.”

As for how she's doing now, Dion told Harper's she's feeling strong, excited and a little nervous—but ready to come back.

Her Paris residency includes 26 concerts running between Sept. 12 and May 29 next year.

World.title: Why everyone is talking about Trump's aide Natalie Harp
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When U.S. President Donald Trump used a catering truck to secretly move from Air Force One during a potential security threat in Turkey early last month, a number of people remained on the plane.

They included U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and the 13-person press pool.

Among those who made the move with Trump: deputy chief of staff Dan Scavino, director of Oval Office operations Walt Nauta and the woman who is suddenly in the middle of a U.S. media firestorm: executive assistant Natalie Harp.

Who is Natalie Harp?

The 35-year-old is special assistant and executive assistant to the president. She can often be seen by his side both in the Oval Office and when he travels. She went to court with him when he was facing trials and was at both 2024 assassination attempts.

Fox News said in a profile shortly after Trump won his second term that Harp has been alongside the president since 2022.

"I believe she is an extra set of eyes and ears for President Trump," Sen. John Barrasso, a Republican from Wyoming, told Fox News then. "Every time I have been with him, she has been close at hand." He added: "If he doesn't pick up the phone, I know to go to Natalie, and he gets the message."

Harp has set up a mobile office that travels with Trump, including a mobile printer to get articles in front of him immediately when needed.

U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, left, and Harp speak with U.S. President Donald Trump at a golf course in Washington, D.C., on June 28. (Ken Cedeno/Reuters)

She first became part of Trump's world in 2019, after the bone cancer survivor lauded the president for a 2018 law meant to give patients access to experimental treatments before approval.

Multiple Republicans have stressed her loyalty to the president, and she speaks of him in glowing terms.

In the Fox profile, she said: "He is on a totally different plane, at peace with God and unshakably focused. Nothing gets to him, because he puts his comfort second and his purpose first."

New York Times reporters Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, in their book Regime Change: Inside the Imperial Presidency of Donald Trump, said Harp alarmed the U.S. Secret Service during the election campaign by leaving Trump adoring letters in his private quarters, including one that said, "You are all that matters to me."

Why is she in the news now?

Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff.

The Georgia senator is running for re-election and has been floated as a presidential candidate, though he denies any interest in the campaign for 2028.

Sen. Jon Ossoff of Georgia speaks at a rally for U.S. presidential candidate Kamala Harris in Atlanta on Oct. 19, 2024. (Dustin Chambers/Reuters)

At a campaign event on Sunday, Ossoff said that Trump doesn't want to do the job.

"He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenceless flying palace gifted by the emir of Qatar," he said, referring in turn to White House renovations, Harp and Air Force One.

Trump's response

On Monday, a reporter in the Oval Office asked Trump about Ossoff's comments.

"You mean Pee-wee Herman?" Trump said. "Pee-wee Herman look-alike. No, I would much rather do other things. It's a — we're building a great facility here. We're fixing a White House that hasn't been taken care of."

White House communications director Steven Cheung used vulgar terms to describe Ossoff and said he was the biggest "loser" in politics. Conservative commentators accused Ossoff of sexism and, given Harp's cancer history, heartlessness.

Tiffany Trump's husband, Michael Boulos, left, Harp and Trump are shown through windows on Marine One as it lands on the South Lawn of the White House on Sept. 18, 2025. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

Democrats and other people opposed to Trump have been giddy about Ossoff's comments, or at least willing to play along. "Ok I'll bite," Michigan state Senate majority whip Mallory McMorrow wrote on X. "Who's Natalie."

The Pod Save America podcast, which is hosted by former Obama speechwriters and aides, said it was mission accomplished for Ossoff because his comments went viral online and made news while winking at rumours there is more than a presidential-staffer relationship. (There is no evidence of any improper relationship.)

"I think there's a question of whether it might kick up media coverage of these allegations now in a way that is frustrating to the White House," said co-host Tommy Vietor.

World.title: They met as teens and felt an instant connection. Decades later, DNA proved they’re actually sisters
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | Meena Geltink describes the remarkable discovery: As It Happens 7:47 They met as teens and felt an instant connection. Decades later DNA proved they’re actually sisters

More than four decades ago, somewhere amid the bustling streets of Mumbai, India, two baby girls were born.

Adopted by different families in the Netherlands, Meena Geltink, 43, and Minal Tijssen, 44, grew up mere hours away from each other.

But their paths never crossed until one day in 1996, when as teenagers, they happened to attend an event organized for adoptees in the Netherlands.

They only met because their friends spotted them first and noticed an uncanny resemblance between the two girls. Not to mention the pair felt an instant connection, Geltink says.

“We spoke, we went to the bathroom, we looked at the mirror, and I saw her, and I thought, ‘Oh my gosh, she has my nose and she has my eyes,'” Geltink told As It Happens guest host Saroja Coehlo. “And we laughed about it.”

But the possibility that they could actually be sisters?

“We wished and we talked about it,” Geltink recalled.

The pair exchanged contact information that day, then kept in touch through letters and emails.

Meena Geltink (top right, bottom left) as a child and Minal Tijssen (top left, bottom right) as a child. (Submitted by Meena Geltink)

But life, as it often does, got in the way. The friends slowly lost touch for nearly three decades.

Eventually, both women started families and Tijssen moved to France.

During those 28 years, Geltink says she joined another adoptee group in the Netherlands for people adopted from India, many of whom had taken MyHeritage DNA tests. In 2017, she decided to give it a shot, too.

“I thought, oh, wow, maybe there is someone out there, some relatives,” she said. “I was just curious about it.”

But it wasn’t until April that the test would change both women’s lives.

Minal Tijssen (left) and Meena Geltink (right) as teens in a picture taken inside a Utrecht photo booth after they met up for a day of shopping. (Submitted by Meena Geltink)

Geltink says she was putting her son to bed when she got a Facebook message from Tijssen, who had taken the test this year.

“She said, ‘Hey, do you remember me? I’m Minal. We shared some letters when we were young,'” Geltink recalled. “She said, ‘Maybe we are sisters because I got a DNA match. Is this your profile on MyHeritage?’”

As it turned out, Geltink had also received the same notification from MyHeritage: a 100 per cent probability that she and Tijssen were sisters.

The test showed they shared 36.5 per cent of their DNA — consistent with the pair being full siblings.

Minal Tijssen (left) and Meena Geltink (right) as teens in Tijssen's parents' backyard in 1996. (Submitted by Meena Geltink)

According to MyHeritage spokesperson Margaux Stelman, such a discovery is rare even for the genealogy platform, particularly given the “unbelievable chain of coincidences” that led the women to each other.

“While it’s more common for people who connect with close family through MyHeritage DNA to find half-siblings, parents, or extended relatives, having two full sisters unknowingly grow up in the same circle is exceptionally rare,” Stelman said in a statement to CBC News.

PHOTOS | Meena Geltink and Minal Tijssen meet for the first time since discovering they're related:

Earlier this month, in a park in Den Bosch, Netherlands, the long-lost siblings met in person for the first time since discovering they were related. Happy tears flowed freely, along with the realization, Geltink says, that each sister had finally found what — or who — they had been subconsciously looking for all their lives.

“In our young years, we felt a little bit lonely sometimes and searching for that one thing we didn’t have,” said Geltink. “And I felt it with her and she felt it with me as well."

"We didn’t know that we were real sisters back then and now everything fell into place. I thought, ‘You’re my missing puzzle piece.’”

She says both of their partners were also there for the emotional reunion; the moment made even more special by the realization the sisters now have each other to lean on for both the difficult and happy times in life.

“In that moment, when I grabbed her and all those tears were just falling from eyes, it was just an amazing moment,��” said Geltink. “I thought, I’m never going to let you go now.”

World.title: Robin Williams's children revive late actor's Instagram amid 'rampant AI abuse'
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Robin Williams’s children have revived the late actor and comedian’s long-dormant Instagram account amid a rise in unauthorized AI likenesses of their father.

Williams died on Aug. 11, 2014, at the age of 63. An autopsy report found he had Lewy body dementia.

"As technology evolves, we want this to be a safe, trusted place where the stories, photos, videos, and memories shared reflect his legacy with authenticity, warmth, and care," Zak, Zelda and Cody Williams wrote in a post on Monday, which was the first on the "therobinwilliams" Instagram account since July 31, 2014.

"This is our way of sharing his unique talent and humor with the world, including the moments that made us and so many of you laugh, as we remember our Dad’s extraordinary life and work. He continues to inspire us and delight people all over the world."

Williams had a prolific career across film, television and stage. He first rose to fame in the television sitcom Mork & Mindy (1978-82) and went on to star in films such as Good Morning Vietnam (1987), Dead Poets Society (1989), Mrs. Doubtfire (1993) and Jumanji (1995).

He won an Academy Award for best supporting actor for his role in Good Will Hunting (1997), and a special achievement Golden Globe Award for voicing Genie in Aladdin (1992).

AI-generated videos of Williams that have appeared online show him on podcasts, performing stand-up comedy routines, giving pep talks and commenting on the dinosaurs in Jurassic Park. Many of the videos were made with OpenAI’s video creation and social media app, Sora.

OpenAI shut down Sora in March. The app was met with an outcry from family estates after people used it to generate videos of public figures such as Michael Jackson, Mister Rogers and Martin Luther King Jr. doing outlandish things.

Daughter vocal in AI opposition

Zelda Williams, an actor and director herself, has long denounced AI recreations of her father.

Last year, she begged fans to stop sending her AI videos of her dad, calling them "disgusting" and saying it’s not what he would have wanted. They echo comments she made in 2023.

In an Instagram story on Monday, she said reviving her father’s Instagram account is part of an effort to fight back against AI.

"I’m sorry if anyone found Dad’s old page posting again to be triggering. Believe me, I know it’s a little strange," she said.

"Making that space into one where people can find authentic clips and photos of him is one of the best ways we’ve now found to fight back against rampant AI abuse of his voice and likeness on here."

Zelda Williams, right, has reacted negatively to AI-generated videos of her late father, Robin. (Ethan Miller/Getty Images, Amy Sussman/Getty Images)

But actor Matthew Lawrence, who co-starred with Williams in Mrs. Doubtfire, told Entertainment Weekly last year that he would like to revive Williams’s voice with AI.

"I would love to do something really special with his voice, because I know for a generation, that voice is just so iconic," he said. "He’s got to be the voice of AI."

But Lawrence said he would only do such a project with permission from the Williams family.

Bernice King, Martin Luther King Jr.’s daughter, has also spoken out against the use of her father in AI.

An AI version of actor Val Kilmer, who died last year at age 65, will star in the upcoming film As Deep As the Grave. Kilmer's estate gave permission for his digital replication and is receiving compensation.

World.title: Ford's Texas trip to talk trade, tariffs cost taxpayers over $93K, internal document reveals
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford's spring trip to Texas to talk trade and tariffs cost taxpayers just over $93,000, a decision note obtained by CBC News through a freedom of information request reveals.

The total cost for the multi-day trip, including a two-day "advance mission" to finalize its logistics, was $93,179, according to the decision note.

"All efforts have been made to maximize outcomes and minimize costs," the document says.

According to the note, those cost-saving measures included the following:

Securing the Ontario Teachers Pension Plan as a sponsor, reducing costs by $7,500.

Hosting a reception, rather than a dinner or lunch, at a venue that had low rental and catering costs.

Keeping staffing "to a minimum."

Securing hotel rooms at government rates.

Ford visited Houston, Dallas and Austin during the trip. He mainly met with business leaders and companies. His expected meeting with Texas governor and longtime Trump ally Greg Abbott did not happen.

WATCH | What you should know about Ford's Texas trip: Everything you need to know about Ford’s visit to Texas | Duration 4:03 Ontario Premier Doug Ford is in Texas meeting politicians and business leaders to discuss trade with Ontario. CBC’s Lorenda Reddekopp breaks down what we know about the trip and what Texans are saying about tariffs.

Groundwork laid for new investment: premier's office

The premier's office defended Ford's trip, telling CBC News that Texas and Ontario have a "long-standing trade relationship that benefits families, workers and businesses on both sides of the border."

"While in Texas, the premier met with over 10 major employers and laid the groundwork for billions of dollars of new investment, more good-paying jobs, and stronger economic ties between Ontario and the United States," it said in an emailed statement Tuesday.

The office also said the province's trade with Texas makes up nearly half of Canada's total trade with the state, and Texas is ranked number two in exports to Ontario and number four in imports from Ontario.

Opposition leaders, meanwhile, slammed the premier's trip, calling it a waste of money.

NDP Leader Marit Stiles said she hasn't seen "any indication" that the trip brought in "any investment."

"It sounds like the most expensive trip to Texas I've ever heard of," she said.

"Nothing seems to explain that kind of price tag."

Interim Liberal Leader John Fraser called the trip a "dog and pony show."

"I'm not sure what was achieved down there. I know he didn't meet with the governor," said Fraser, adding he'd like to see the results of the trip and what investments were brought back to Ontario.

"The thing I'd like to see is the premier actually travelling to places like Japan or India or Europe, we know that we have to diversify our partnerships," he said.

WATCH | Trump paused 50% tariffs hours before they took effect: Trump pauses 50% tariffs, saying new trade deal reached | Duration 6:27 U.S. President Donald Trump has paused 50 per cent tariffs on Canada, saying the two countries have reached a new trade deal that just needs to be finalized. In a statement, Prime Minister Mark Carney said 'substantial progress has been made.'

Green Party of Ontario Leader Mike Schreiner said Ford needs to travel in a way that's "transparent and honest" with taxpayers.

"I'm all for the premier going to the U.S. and defending Ontario. What I'm not for is a government that's going to try and waste our tax dollars on private luxury jets, fancy hotel rooms and expensive dinners," he said.

The decision note did not provide a breakdown of the trip cost. CBC News asked the premier's office for a breakdown of the expenses, but it did not provide one in its response.

World.title: Colombia’s government publishes “white paper” on corruption by Petro
World.content:
The government of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella gave Prosecutor General Luz Adriana Camargo a white paper with more than 80 complaints over alleged corruption by the previous government.

The 135-page “Book of Truth that was presented by De la Espriella, contained “the result of the work carried out under the coordination of Vice President José Manuel Restrepo during the transition weeks between the presidential election and August 7” when he took office.

De la Espriella suspended the transition process on July 7 after Petro said he refused to recognize the president as his legitimate successor.

Consequently, the book contains mainly political criticisms of the previous “regime” and no evidence of misdeeds that hadn’t been picked by the Comptroller General’s Office, which monitors public spending.

This white paper, my fellow Colombians, does not intend to replace, far less anticipate, judicial investigations or the outcome of actions taken by prosecutors, inspectors, and comptrollers. The book actually represents something simpler and, at the same time, more serious, monumental, and decisive: the fulfillment of my duty as Head of State. I am fulfilling the responsibility that falls upon me by gathering available information and not allowing the facts recorded here in the book I have just delivered to be buried by silence and impunity. The duty of a leader is to bring the truth to the doorstep of justice and stop there, scrupulously respecting the independence and majesty of the judicial system. That moment has arrived. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president blamed the budget deficit on the “sacking” of the Petro administration rather than Congress’s failure to approve the legislation that allowed the previous government to carry out its 2026 budget.

De la Espriella previously said he would extradite Petro if the US Government asked him to.

World.title: Colombia says 377 still missing three days after 7.4M earthquake
World.content:
The director of Colombia’s disaster management agency UNGRD said Thursday that at least 273 people died and that 377 were missing from the region that was struck by a 7.4M earthquake on Monday.

According to UNGRD director David Tamayo, the earthquake affected a total of 97,515 people.

So far, rescue workers and neighbors were able to rescue 348 people from the rubble alive and 3,826 people were injured.

The earthquake, which was the strongest in a decade, destroyed 12,563 homes and damaged another 75,654.

At least 172 apartment buildings collapsed, said Tamayo.

Damaged public infrastructure

217 health centers and hospitals

2,206 educational facilities

825 community centers

226 roads

71 aqueducts

24 vehicular bridges

8 pedestrian bridges

5 airports

The disaster triggered President Abelardo de la Espriella to declare an economic emergency in the disaster area, and in the southern Putumayo and the eastern Norte de Santander province where no damages were reported.

This State of Exception allows the president to govern by decree when it comes to matters related to disaster relief and reconstruction in the affected area.

The State of Exception will last three months and can be extended by another three with congressional approval.

World.title: Colombia declares economic emergency to rebuild after earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella said he would declare an economic emergency and create a reconstruction fund for homes and small businesses that were destroyed in Monday’s earthquake.

In a press statement, De la Espriella said that the government would initially support victims with temporary relief and will declare an economic emergency to find the funds for reconstruction.

Finance Minister Miguel Gomez said the government was not yet considering raising taxes to find the approximately COP20 trillion ($6.4 billion) that would at least be needed for reconstruction.

The president said his government would initially prioritize relief for the estimated 24,000 families from the west of the country who have lost their homes or businesses.

The temporary relief measures would include:

The payment of public services for affected families by the government.

Housing rent subsidies for those who lost their homes.

Tax and financial relief measures.

Economic support for the most vulnerable families.

Support mechanisms for merchants and small business owners who have been affected by the earthquake.

As part of the emergency, De la Espriella announced the creation of a “Miracle Fund, an entity that will channel national and international contributions destined for the reconstruction of hospitals, educational centers, properties, roads, and airports that suffered damage from the earthquake.”

“The state of emergency must encompass economic reactivation measures that stimulate investment, reduce obstacles to project development, and generate more jobs in the affected areas,” said the president.

An economic emergency gives the president three months to issue decrees related to the cause of the emergency without having to go through Congress.

The legal validity of the decree declaring an emergency and those that follow will only be tested by the Constitutional Court.

At the time of publication the President’s Office had yet to issue its first decree.

World.title: Colombia asked US to carry out joint military operations: Hegseth
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella asked the US Government for joint military operations “to destroy terrorists and terror networks,” said US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth Wednesday.

At an event of the so-called Americas Counter Cartel Coalition (ACCC) in Panama, Hegseth said that “Colombia will join the ACCC, becoming the 19th member.”

Through the newly inaugurated president, as our president likes to say “President El Tigre,” Colombia has already requested that our department of war join Colombia in its fight against narcoterrorism. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth

Hegseth’s announcement was rejected by leftist opposition party Historic Pact, whose Senate chief Ivan Cepeda said that “the US citizen Abelardo de la Espriella wants to surrender our government, our territory and our sovereignty to the strategic interests of the United States.

Cepeda stressed that Colombia’s constitution allows only the Senate to permit the entry of foreign troops to the country.

Colombia’s sovereignty is not up for negotiation, it is not to be surrendered, and it cannot be subordinated to the military interests of any foreign power. To defend it is to defend the dignity of the nation, the independence of the Republic, and the right of the Colombian people to freely decide on their territory and their destiny. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Ahead of taking office on Friday, De la Espriella said that he would join US-led alliances that allegedly seek to combat drug trafficking.

In his inaugural speech, the president said he intends to “defeat, without truce, narco-terrorism and all criminal organizations that threaten the freedom of Colombia.”

The State Department last week announced that it would seek to send a $1 billion military aid package to Colombia to “support the De la Espriella Administration’s efforts to defeat the vicious narcoterrorist and criminal organizations that threaten US, Colombian, and hemispheric security and economic prosperity.”

World.title: Controversy in Colombia over refusal to allow foreign search and rescue teams
World.content:
The government of President Abelardo de la Espriella has been criticized over its refusal to accept foreign search and rescue workers in the crucial hours after Monday’s earthquake.

One of the first to raise the alarm was China’s ambassador to Bogota, Zhu Jingyang, who called on the government on Tuesday to “release the name of the official and his or her designated contact person to coordinate international aid for the earthquake victims.”

El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele said that he was told that Colombia’s “rescue teams, medical personnel, and other emergency responders are on the scene and handling the situation” and “they do not require personnel support.”

Mexico’s President Caudia Sheinbaum said that her government was waiting for approval to send a team of 225 rescue workers to look for survivors, but was waiting for a “formal invitation” from Bogota.

In a response to growing pressure, newspaper El Tiempo said Colombia didn’t need foreign search and rescue teams because “the country has 23 teams with personnel that is part of the global elite.”

The Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday evening that it had “called on the international community to provide support in addressing the emergency, in order to tackle the most severely affected areas and mitigate the disaster.”

But social leader Leonard Renteria from Buenaventura said Wednesday that “as of yesterday, we still didn’t know anything about the arrival of rescue workers” in the partially destroyed port city.

“On the streets, we’ve seen people from the neighborhoods with the firefighters and civil defense personnel,” Renteria posted on social media platform X.

Fifty hours after Monday’s disaster, the US Department of State said it had “mobilized urban search-and-rescue (USAR) technical teams from Fairfax County, Virginia, and Los Angeles County, California to support Colombia’s search and rescue efforts.”

With chances of finding people alive rapidly decreasing, pressure on the government to respond increased online.

“I would really like to know the technical reason for rejecting assistance from teams that specialize in this type of disaster. There are many affected areas and plenty of evidence of technical inadequacies,” said civil engineer Gina Villalobos on X.

According to opposition congresswoman Maria Fernanda Carrascal, “it was an ideological decision, they only wanted rescue workers from Israel and the United States to enter while the Mexicans have been ready since Monday.”

On Wednesday afternoon, newly appointed disaster response chief David Tamayo said the government would also allow search and rescue workers from Ecuador and El Salvador “that can guarantee the provision of search and rescue teams and that are recognized by their own governments as meeting international search and rescue standards.”

These teams would come to search for hundreds of people who are feared to be under the rubble of buildings that collapsed in the worst earthquake in 10 years.

World.title: West Colombia earthquake killed more than 227 people, say local authorities
World.content:
Local and regional authorities have said that at least 227 people were confirmed killed in Monday’s earthquake while search and rescue teams continue to look for survivors.

So far, 120 people were confirmed dead in Valle del Cauca where locals said that entire towns in the north of the province were all but destroyed by the 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck the Choco province on Monday.

In Cali, the capital of Valle del Cauca, rescue workers continued to look for survivors under the rubble of apartment buildings that collapsed. Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder imposed a curfew in the city after locals chased him away from a search and rescue operation.

Choco Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said that mayors from the capital Quibdo and 22 affected towns reported 14 deaths and 140 injuries.

Multiple parts of the western province have yet to be contacted, however, as the local energy and telephone grid were destroyed by the earthquake, said Cordoba.

In Pereira, a city located at only 60 kilometers of the earthquake’s epicenter, and the surrounding Risaralda province, at least 88 people had died and dozens were still missing.

All major cities in the coffee region, Choco and Valle del Cauca declared an emergency to deal with the hundreds of injured that required medical attention at one of the cities’ hospitals.

President Abelardo de la Espriella said Tuesday morning that the earthquake destroyed more than 5,000 homes and that 188 people were missing.

The National Army and fire brigades from across Colombia sent teams to the cities in the disaster area to help with local search and rescue missions.

The US Department of State said it had committed $15.5 million “in funding for emergency shelter, food, protection, and earthquake assessments” for Colombia.

The Chinese embassy in Bogota said that Chinese companies that operate in Colombia were “sending heavy equipment to the most affected areas of the earthquake, participating in rescue efforts and the clearing of debris, in order to rescue the affected population using all available means.”

World.title: Colombia declares national disaster after devastating earthquake
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella declared a national disaster and sent his ministers to the west of Colombia to coordinate rescue operations in response to a 7.4M earthquake.

Following an emergency meeting at disaster management agency UNGRD, De la Espriella said he would travel to Pereira, one of the worst hit cities, to further coordinate the government response.

Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara would coordinate rescue operations for the rest of the coffee region, the health and defense ministers would travel to the Choco and Transport Minister Elsa Noguera would coordinate efforts in Valle del Cauca from Cali.

De la Espriella canceled plans he had to visit La Guajira, a northern province that wasn’t affected by the earthquake.

Throughout the morning, local and regional media reported dozens of collapsed buildings in multiple cities in Valle del Cauca, the coffee region and Choco.

More than 110 people were killed and dozens were injured because of the earthquake, De la Espriella said at a press conference.

The earthquake damaged more than 1,500 homes and destroyed 37. Sixty-one buildings collapsed and 18 healthcare centers suffered damage as well as 52 schools and 17 community centers.

The roof of the Pereira airport also came down and five other airports in western Colombia reported damages, said the president.

According to the National Police, road travel has been complicated because of landslides and fallen trees.

The government has yet to report on missing persons.

“Right now, the most important thing is to protect lives, rescue those who remain trapped, treat the injured, and bring aid to the hardest-hit communities,” said Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo.

“United we will overcome this emergency,” Restrepo added.

The vice-president, together with Foreign Minister Omar Bula, will coordinate foreign aid.

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade and the strongest in the west of the country since 1979.

World.title: 7.4M earthquake hits western Colombia: at least 110 killed, dozens of buildings collapsed
World.content:
An M7.4 earthquake hit western Colombia on Monday, killing at least 110 people and injuring hundreds.

The earthquake struck around 7:30 and had its epicenter in San Jose del Palmar, a municipality in the Choco province.

In the hour that followed, locals began reporting collapsed buildings in the cities of Cali, Pereira and Manizales, where a tower of the cathedral and a dozen other buildings fully or partially collapsed, according to Mayor Jorge Eduardo Rojas.

In a first report on fatalities, Risaralda Governor Juan Diego Patiño said that at least 40 people were killed in the capital Perira. Another three would have been killed in Manizales.

In Cali, an unknown number of people would be trapped under the rubble of multiple buildings. At least 27 people would be killed in the Valle del Cauca province.

Large parts of the roof of the Pereira airport came down, according to video shared on social media.

Flights to Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura were suspended while airport authorities check for damages to infrastructure

In Quibdo, the capital of Choco, at least four people were killed and another 69 were injured, Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said in her second report.

The earthquake was also felt strongly in the capital Bogota and in Medellin where no injuries were reported.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said on social media platform X that he had “personally taken charge of the emergency response in San José del Palmar.”

“I will also be in Pereira in person to stand with those affected and monitor the government’s response,” said De la Espriella, who took office on Friday and has yet to appoint his director of disaster response agency UNGRD.

The president later reported that he was on his way to Bogota to lead rescue efforts from the UNGRD’s main office.

I have established a Unified Command Post at the UNGRD, from where I will personally lead the efforts to assist the communities in Chocó, the Coffee Region, and all affected areas. President Abelardo de la Espriella

According to the Colombian Geological Service, the earthquake was the strongest in Colombia of the past decade.

World.title: Evacuations ordered in Chile as wildfires run amok
World.content:
Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred) Wednesday ordered the evacuation of 14 communes in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, including Nacimiento, Purén, and Contulmo, which have all been particularly affected by the forest fires.

In messages broadcast through the Emergency Alert System (SAE), the authorities also called on residents to leave their homes to avoid further damage to their health.

It has already been a week since the first wildfires ran amok in south-central Chile despite efforts to contain them. High temperatures, dryness, and strong winds add to the plight of local people and some 5,600 firefighters deployed in the area while helping flocks in from abroad.

”We are entering this part of the week which is the most complex. Today, tomorrow, and the day after we have an alert for high temperatures in several regions of the country that has mobilized a very large effort (…) to prevent the fires from spreading,“ Interior Minister Carolina Tohá said regarding the 311 active fires, of which 89 are being fought. The Senapred also said 180 fires were under control, and 309,747 hectares have been affected.

”If the temperature rises and the wind increases we can indeed have more problems, and we already have many fires,” Spanish Lieutenant Colonel Carlos Javier Martín Traverso told AFP. Traverso’s Air Operations Section of the Military Emergency Unit (UME) arrived in Chile on Sunday to join the firefighting efforts.

Over 309,000 hectares have been consumed in the regions of Maule, Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía with the death toll standing at 24, plus 2,180 people injured as 1,180 houses were destroyed, leaving 5,560 people homeless.

There seems to be a seamless scientific consensus that fires are the result of human actions, either by intentionality or carelessness, although the drought that has hit Chile for 13 years adds to the aggressiveness of the fires.

In this scenario, President Gabriel Boric Font has announced a curfew in the areas of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía where a state of catastrophe is in force, in order to guarantee the security and tranquility of

the families affected by the crisis. Defense authorities working on the sites will determine the restriction’s schedule.

“We have 24 people dead nationwide, three are from Santa Juana and we do not want there to be even one more,” Boric told reporters after visiting the area.

The number of fatalities was updated to 24 after two bodies were determined to belong to people who had died before the fires broke out.

Meanwhile, Biobío Governor Rodrigo Díaz said he was certain about “people criminally setting fires.”

“I have reports from police, firefighters, of people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols,” he insisted in a radio interview.

“We have fire outbreaks at the southern exit of Contulmo, different places where fires were set 300 meters away from each other, I could see it, nobody told me about it. The mayor of Mulchén told me how fires were lit in the four cardinal points, I have reports from the police, the Fire Department, from people who have been setting fires. I do not have indications, but certainties, we need more patrols in the area,” he explained.

President Boric’s Regional Delegate Daniela Dresdner said eight people had been arrested for “irresponsible and suspicious attitudes with respect to the setting of fires. This was due to citizen complaints and patrols by the Navy.”

“We are asking that all these conducts be denounced and we are filing a lawsuit for all these denunciations to [be] prosecute[d],” she added.

The Biobío Regional Prosecutor’s Office called on the citizenry to e-mail all data regarding criminal behavior to fiscaliaincendios@gmail.com, including pictures, videos, audios, or written information as to the probable causes of the fires, which will be handled confidentially. (Merco Press)

World.title: Chile’s wildfires death toll reaches 24
World.content:
Chilean authorities spoke Sunday of 24 fatalities, nearly 1,000 people injured, and some 800 houses destroyed in the past five days by wildfires spreading fast in amid a highly-irregular heat wave with strong winds and temperatures above 40°C in areas 500 km south of Santiago.

The death toll reached 24 after the death of one of the injured people who had been hospitalized in Angol, Undersecretary of the Interior Manuel Monsalve explained. “The risk situation in the country remains” in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío, and La Araucanía, and in certain localities of the central region of Maule, he said. A red alert was also decreed Sunday in communes of the southern regions of Los Ríos and Los Lagos due to the appearance of new fire outbreaks. He also pointed out that 26 of the 997 people injured were in serious condition.

“I came home from work and I was already without anything, without a house. I was left on the street, with my arms crossed, now with my son, and my wife, in a tent. I have no fodder for my animals,” a resident of the town of Purén, in the Araucanía region, told Televisión Nacional de Chile (TVN).

Meanwhile, President Gabriel Boric Font attended the wake of a firefighter in the town of Coronel. ”Chile is crying with you. I am here to tell you that you are not alone, that the family of Yesenia (Muñoz, the deceased firefighter) will not be alone,” he said.

According to Chile’s National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response (Senapred), the number of fires being fought went down from 87 to 51. “We are experiencing a small window of improving weather conditions during Sunday and Monday. That means that we are not with extremely high temperatures,” Monsalve said.

Undersecretary Monsalve also told reporters that 10 people have been arrested for their responsibility in starting some of the fires for which the red alert was still maintained. Of the total number of fires, 22 occurred Sunday for a total of 283 active fires, of which 151 were under control and 71 are being fought.

Given the magnitude of the fires in size and number, international help has been summoned. “We have just sent a plane to Chile with a contingent of the Military Emergency Unit to collaborate in extinguishing and controlling the fires that are raging in the country. All our support to the Chilean people,” tweeted Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

Chile’s Foreign Ministry also said assistance was being coordinated with Argentina, Brazil, Ecuador, the United States, and Mexico, while Boric’s administration has declared a constitutional state of catastrophe in the regions of Ñuble, Biobío and La Araucanía, to speed up additional resources while restricting free transit and involving military forces to contain the disaster.

In 2017, another chain of fires destroyed some 460,000 hectares, left 11 people dead, nearly 6,000 injured, and more than 1,500 homes burned.

Monsalve also warned that this week high temperatures will continue, as well as the risk of low humidity and strong gusts of wind, which will make it difficult to extinguish the flames. – MercoPress

World.title: Parts of Chile under red alert for major forest fires in central region
World.content:
The Government of Chile has declared a “red alert” in the central part of the country due to the heat wave stemming from 39 major forest fires as the wave keeps spreading throughout the country, most of them in Araucania (17) but also in Bío Bío (7), Ñuble (7), Maule (4), Los Lagos (3), and one in the Santiago Metropolitan Region.

The National Service for Disaster Prevention and Response reported that in addition to the 39 fires currently being fought, there were four others under observation, while 141 were already under control, and 20 had already been extinguished.

Authorities ordered a series of preventive evacuations in several towns, as well as the interruption of highway traffic in the most affected areas where 181 hectares of scrubland and pastureland were burned out, threatening nearby homes.

The main cause for the fires is said to be the summer high temperatures which reached 41 degrees Celsius in the Chillán area.

Meteorologists forecast that the heat wave will last until Sunday. The last major fires to affect Chile were recorded in the summer of 2017 when the flames swept through entire villages, causing 11 deaths and more than 580 thousand hectares affected.

The state-owned National Forestry Corporation (Conaf) reported that in the Ñuble region, the fire has already affected some 550 hectares in the area of Chillán Viejo and another 200 hectares in another town near the regional capital, burning infrastructure and some houses.

Agriculture Minister Esteban Valenzuela told reporters that in addition to the heat wave, the dry and hot Puelche wind from the eastern cordillera was also expected in the central-southern zone. Valenzuela also announced the temporary closure of seven national parks from Santiago to the south in the Metropolitan, Ñuble, Biobío, La Araucanía, and Aysén regions to prevent new fires, and also ordered the evacuation of rural areas of Ñuble, where simultaneous forest fires were reported.

– MercoPress

World.title: Chilean airlines will reimburse cost of boarding taxes under certain conditions
World.content:
Chile’s national Consumer Service, Sernac is calling all consumers who purchased tickets directly from airlines between 2015 and 201l and did not make use of them, to claim from the companies the reimbursement of the boarding taxes paid.

Following on a Voluntary Collective Procedure reached at the beginning of 2020 with LATAM, and at the end of 2021 with Sky, Avianca, Jetsmart, Aerolineas Argentinas and COPA, the airlines agreed to reimburse the boarding taxes cost for flights not done between May first 2015 and 24 December 2021, with the exception of Jetsmart, which only started operations in Chile in July 2017.

Accordingly the universe of beneficiaries reached 1.108.416 passengers and involved some US$ 12 million for domestic flights and US$ 1,4 million for international flights. The amount to be reimbursed to each potential passenger depends on the distance to travel and if it was domestic of international travel.

In Chile the domestic boarding tax is equivalent to some US$ 14 and overseas US$ 50. Allegedly following the agreement the companies were to inform the beneficiaries of their reimbursements.

Reimbursements can also be checked by filling forms at the airlines’ offices. For further information on the agreement and the sums involved consumers are invited to check the web.

World.title: Remembering Steve Anderson
World.content:
BENJAMIN WITTE

I was neither the first nor the last of the many interns and editors who peopled the office of the Santiago Times during the quarter century founder Steve Anderson captained the ship. But for whatever reason, I stuck around longer than most, and it was with great sadness that I learned yesterday about the automobile accident that ended his life.

My first encounter with Steve came in late 2002, after he had offered me the editor’s job—sight unseen, via e-mail—and I accepted, knowing only that I’d earn about US$500 a month and should show up in Santiago with an AP style guide and a copy of Strunk and White’s The Elements of Style. That it all seemed a bit rushed and loosey-goosey gave me pause for concern, but I was eager for an excuse to return to Chile, so hopped on a plane and flew down from Costa Rica.

Still, after our first meeting, I wondered just how wise my decision really was. It was then that I realized the Santiago Times wasn’t, as I’d imagined, a print paper. It was Internet-based, with a rudimentary website that was only half functioning. “We got hacked,” Steve told me. He also explained that he was living at that moment in Puerto Montt—1,000 kilometers to the south—and that he was recovering still from a recent and quite serious car accident. It had been a very bad year, he said.

I gave the gig a chance, though, and things gradually improved. Some energetic new interns trickled in, as they always did at the Santiago Times. A talented British/Australian writer showed up too, and I asked Steve to hire him as a kind of co-editor. The business couldn’t really afford another paid staff member, but Steve honored my request, and for the next year or so we had a great run. Then the money ran out.

“I can’t afford to pay you both, so one of you has to go,” Steve told us one morning. “I’ll leave it up to you two to decide which one.” And so we did—over a liter of beer, even though it was like nine-something in the morning. The co-editor (still a dear friend of mine) offered to go. But I’d leave too, I decided. A month or so later. The job had run its course, I thought.

We were frustrated and certainly taken aback—especially by the “decide amongst yourselves who stays and goes” part of the equation. And yet, neither of us was really surprised, because even then, we’d seen enough of Steve and his herky-jerky management style to know that this was precisely the kind of situation that could and would, as it turned out, unfold.

We couldn’t really be angry either. Or at least not stay angry. Because again, with Steve, what you saw is what you got. He was passionate about his project, but not always clear about how to make it grow. Often he’d have a new idea, and then charge ahead. And in those cases, there’d be a flurry of positive changes—new computers maybe, a new paid staff person, a larger office space. But then a particularly capable group of interns would move on, money would run scarce, the whole operation would contract, and we’d be back to square one, or so it felt.

I know this because later I joined Steve for a second, longer stint. What never varied, though, was his fighting spirit. A feisty advocate for the underdog, he was always chomping to champion a good cause—demanding accountability for human rights violations, defending the environment, shining a light on corruption and hypocrisy.

The Santiago Times was his platform, and he committed himself tooth-and-nail to making it survive, if not prosper. And in the meantime, the interns, editors, photographers and other collaborators kept coming through. They kept using Steve’s office and humble little publication as a landing point for early-career, working-abroad experiences, and as a launching pad for further adventures and professional endeavors.

If there was a method to Steve’s madcap approach, it was that with each new idea he had for the Santiago Times, with each new push to improve or revive it, he bought the business a little more time. Months turned into years and then decades. And all the while, people like myself were given an opportunity to work and learn—in large part through trial and error, because although Steve had things to teach, he also gave us space to teach ourselves.

It was his special tenacity, though, that kept the whole thing going, that gave so many people the chance, year after year, to develop their skills. We had fun too. So much fun. The office on Av. Santa María produced lasting, globe-spanning friendships, even love stories. And that was also part of Steve’s gift to us all.
