El NWS ha anunciado este miércoles que se mantienen las “alertas de calor extremo” ya vigentes en gran parte del suroeste desértico de Estados Unidos, así como en zonas que abarcan desde las llanuras del sur del país hasta la región conocida como Sur Profundo, concepto que suele englobar la totalidad de los Estados de Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama y Georgia, así como partes de California, Texas, Florida, Arkansas y Tennessee. “Las temperaturas mínimas nocturnas serán tan elevadas (rondando los 27 grados centígrados en algunos casos) que, sumadas a unos puntos de rocío sofocantes, apenas ofrecerán alivio frente a las abrasadoras máximas diurnas”, continúa el Servicio Meteorológico.

El calor no es el único problema derivado del cambio climático que está afectando a grandes estados del país. En un momento en el que la sequía afecta al corazón de Europa, con millones de ciudadanos sufriendo limitaciones inéditas en el acceso al agua y con problemas en el comercio, la agricultura y la energía por el escaso caudal de los grandes ríos, algo parecido ocurre en la zona suroeste de Estados Unidos. La sequía que azota al país ya ha alcanzado cotas importantes, suscitando dudas sobre el suministro de agua y de electricidad a medio plazo. Los lagos Powell y Mead, los embalses más grandes del país, se están secando. Los especialistas no ven ahora cómo salir de la crisis del sistema hídrico que rodea al río Colorado, fuente de agua y electricidad para millones de personas.

El sábado, el nivel del agua en el lago Powell, situado en la frontera entre Utah y Arizona, descendió a un mínimo histórico, según informa The New York Times. Una semana antes, el lago Mead —el mayor de los dos— había alcanzado su punto más bajo jamás registrado. El sistema conjunto de embalses no registraba niveles tan bajos desde 1957. El cambio climático ha contribuido a una sequía que se alarga ya durante décadas, la peor racha de aridez en el suroeste en al menos 1.200 años, según los científicos.

Las autoridades federales y estatales han adoptado medidas de emergencia para tratar de evitar una catástrofe, como ejecutar trasvases desde embalses más pequeños para intentar salvar el lago Powell. También han hecho llamamientos a la conservación del agua. Según datos recogidos por la agencia Efe de la Oficina de Recuperación de Estados Unidos (USBR), el lago Powell, el segundo embalse más grande del país, se sitúa en unos 3.500 pies, unos niveles preocupantes para el suministro energético y de agua en la región. Un estudio de esta agencia realizado en julio aseguraba que las reservas de agua del lago Powell corrían el riesgo de descender hasta el nivel considerado necesario para generar electricidad (unos 3.490 pies).

World.title: Francia registra 7.300 muertes adicionales durante las olas de calor desde mayo
World.content:
Entre el 3 y el 22 de julio hubo 1.243 fallecidos y este verano, además de ser el más caluroso, es ya el más mortífero tras el de 2003, con 15.000 decesos

El verano de 2026 en Francia, sin que haya acabado agosto, pasará ya a la historia como uno de los peores y más mortíferos desde que existen registros. El país contabilizó 1.243 muertos adicionales entre el 3 y el 22 de julio, durante la segunda ola de calor estival, que se suman a los 5.764 decesos registrados del 17 al 30 de junio, en la primera canícula. Esto sitúa el balance provisional en unos 7.300 fallecidos, según informaron este miércoles el Ministerio de Sanidad y la agencia Santé Publique France. Las autoridades advierten que este exceso de mortalidad es por todo tipo de causas y “no se pueden atribuir aún con total seguridad al calor extremo”.

Casi tres cuartas partes de estas muertes en los días más calurosos de julio (917) “corresponden a personas de 75 años o más”, que son “las más vulnerables ante este tipo de episodios”, según recordó Sébastien Denys, director de sanidad en Santé Publique France, durante una conferencia de prensa virtual para presentar los datos. El balance previo se dio el 2 de julio.

Estas muertes afectaron a todos los grupos de edad a partir de los 45 años, según el ministerio de Sanidad, que destacó el incremento de los decesos a domicilio (casi el 26%). La mitad se produjeron en hospitales y un 18% residencias de ancianos.

Francia atraviesa su quinta canícula desde primavera (la tercera del verano), que está remitiendo estos días y es la segunda más larga que se ha vivido nunca, tras 22 días con temperaturas extremadamente altas. Además, el país ha sufrido desde finales de primavera 52 días de ola de sofoco, una cifra también histórica, según Météo France, la agencia de meteorología.

Las olas de calor se han encadenado con tan pocos días de tregua que incluso resulta difícil diferenciarlas. La de junio, que duró 10 días, fue la más intensa que ha habido, peor incluso que la de 2003. Aquel verano fue traumático en el país, pues murieron 15.000 personas por culpa de las altas temperaturas. La canícula de julio ha sido menos dura pero más duradera y además ha afectado a prácticamente todo el país, 78 departamentos del centenar que hay. El 80% de la población estuvo expuesta a las altas temperaturas.

“Todas las regiones han sufrido un exceso de mortalidad, a excepción de la isla de Córcega, que ha estado menos expuesta”, recordó Sébastien Denys, de la agencia de salud. En la conferencia de prensa, las autoridades explicaron la complejidad a la hora de manejar estas estadísticas y establecer un balance de muertes atribuibles al calor.

Los datos muestran el exceso de mortalidad durante estos periodos y hay que tomarlos “con prudencia”. Aún así, son cifras “que dan una idea del impacto sanitario que tienen las canículas en la salud de la población”, detalló Didier Lepelletier, director general de Sanidad. “El verano que estamos viviendo es excepcional en el plano meteorológico, por la intensidad [de las canículas], su precocidad, duración y frecuencia”, ilustró.

El balance completo se publicará en el mes de octubre, cuando acabe el periodo estival, aunque las cifras hasta la fecha, sin tener en cuenta el mes de agosto, convierten este año en el peor tras el de 2003. En 2025 se contabilizaron 1.900 muertes vinculadas a las altas temperaturas en las tres olas de calor que vivió el país y 5.700 entre junio y septiembre.

World.title: Online sleuth links Amsterdam’s “Lucky” to Canadian cold case
World.content:
An online researcher may have made a breakthrough in the hunt for the identity of “Lucky”, a man who collapsed in Amsterdam three years ago and is unable to communicate. A recent public appeal for information by the police has surfaced a potential match with a missing person in Canada.

An image of “Lucky”, who was also known by the name “Chris the Canadian” to Amsterdam locals, was likened to a file of pictures on the Vancouver Police Department’s cold case unit by someone on Facebook.

John Russell Kennedy, whose missing person’s file photos appear very similar to the one the Dutch police put out, was registered as missing since 1993.

Dutch police said they are considering the tip, according to paper AD, though they also noted that such similarities have been common in prior cases and turned out not to be real matches. “We don’t want to jump to any conclusions at this point, or to give false hope,” a spokesperson said.

Much of what is listed on the Canadian missing person’s case matches descriptions put out by locals who knew the man before his collapse in 2023. He was said to have a North American accent and appeared to have mental health problems.

Vancouver police confirmed they are taking the tip very seriously and said they had made contact with Amsterdam police, according to Anton van Straten, the person who made the connection online and shared it via Facebook.

“Only an official investigation, for example using DNA, can provide certainty about this,” Van Straten wrote in his post. “Now it is up to the professionals to investigate this further. In any case, it didn’t take me three years to find this potential match.”

If “Lucky” is indeed John Russell Kennedy, he would be 67 years old now and missing from his family for almost half his life.

World.title: Number of non-EU dentists in NL doubles in five years
World.content:
The number of dentists trained outside the EU who are moving to the Netherlands to help fill a chronic national shortage has more than doubled in five years, with recent arrivals coming from countries including Syria, South Africa, Turkey, Brazil and Iraq.

One in four dentists now working in the country qualified abroad, according to the dentists’ association KNMT, and in Zeeland more than half were trained overseas.

Figures from the Amsterdam dental school ACTA, which runs the admissions process for applicants from outside the EU, show 120 people are sitting its professional competence test this year, compared with 53 in 2021, the current affairs programme Nieuwsuur reported.

In total, 2,287 dentists with a foreign diploma are working in the Netherlands, a number rising by 150 to 200 a year.

Lack of national funding

The reliance on overseas recruits is partly due to a lack of education funding for Dutch students. Thousands apply but places are very limited. Etienne Verheijck, education director for the ACTA, called that “a policy choice by the education ministry.”

KNMT chair Hans de Vries called it “painful” that motivated young people are rejected by a lottery system, sometimes three times in a row, while the gap is filled from abroad.

The shortage is expected to grow, and the government’s own capacity advisory body has for years urged ministers to open more training places.

Checking your dentist is registered

To work in the Netherlands, dentists with a non-EU diploma must pass a competence test and learn Dutch before they can join the official BIG register of healthcare professionals. Those with an EU diploma need only meet the language requirement.

The healthcare inspectorate IGJ said it regularly receives reports of people performing treatments such as root canals without being registered. De Vries said dentists may work under a registered colleague’s supervision while they qualify, but treating patients unsupervised is improper and potentially unlawful.

Patients can check whether their own dentist appears on the BIG register, which is public and free to search. Dental care in the Netherlands works differently from many other countries, and full practices unable to take on new patients are already a common complaint.

A 12-year-old Dutch boy is being treated in intensive care after falling 30 metres (100ft) while walking in the Austrian alps.

Local media reported that the boy was walking with his father when he slipped and fell while crossing rocky terrain in the Tirol mountain range at 11am on Tuesday.

The pair were descending the Gänsekragen mountain after reaching the 2,914m (9,560ft) summit at 9.30am.

They were walking along a waymarked path towards a mountain hut in Winnebachsee when the accident happened about 500m below the summit as the boy rounded a corner.

The 46-year-old man managed to climb down the hillside to his son, who was lying unconscious, and raise the alarm. An air ambulance transported him to a clinic in Innsbruck, where he is being treated for serious injuries.

Police are investigating how the boy fell.

World.title: Schiphol security staff begin strike action over workload
World.content:
Security staff at Schiphol will begin short work stoppages and deliberately slow-downs in the coming days, after the airport and its three security firms missed a union deadline to ease a workload the unions say has become unmanageable. Travellers could face longer queues as a result.

Unions FNV and CNV announced the action on Wednesday, after an ultimatum to Schiphol and the firms Securitas, I-SEC and Trigion expired at midday. The stoppages will be flagged only a few hours in advance, and the unions have not ruled out longer strikes if nothing changes.

“Nobody wants industrial action at Schiphol,” said CNV negotiator André Quist. “But if employers take no concrete step against the enormous workload even after a crystal-clear ultimatum, they leave our members no choice.”

The dispute dates back to a shake-up in the spring, when Schiphol cut the number of firms running hand-baggage checks from five to three. The switch to new employers affected most of the airport’s roughly 5,000 security guards, whose pay was preserved but whose rosters, shift times, breaks and leave all changed.

Since then, the unions say, workloads have risen and sickness absence has climbed, leaving fewer guards to carry the same load – a downward spiral they warn is getting worse.

In July the unions made eight demands, including longer breaks, two consecutive days off after five worked, a heat protocol for the terminals, and at least two women on every security lane so female passengers can be searched. A lane should close, they say, if only one woman is available.

Schiphol said it regretted the action and took the guards’ concerns seriously, adding that it and the three firms were already working on improvements to five of the eight demands. It said it would do all it could to limit the impact on travellers.

A separate walkout by around 350 cleaners at the airport also happened on Wednesday for two hours around midday in a dispute over reduced sick pay in the national cleaning agreement, which FNV wants Schiphol, as a major client, to help resist.

The return leg in Amsterdam next Thursday, August 27, will be screen on Ziggo’s free subscription channel.

On Wednesday, NEC Nijmegen will be hoping to take a step towards the Champions League group stages as they host Norwegian side Bodø/Glimt in the first leg of their play-off tie. The match is being shown on Ziggo Sport, with the return leg in Norway next Tuesday, August 25.

World.title: Criminals cashing in on black market for non-deposit cans
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Criminal gangs are earning millions by importing canned drinks to bypass the Dutch deposit return system.

The black market has sprung up since a compulsory 15 cent deposit was imposed on all drinks cans in 2023, as part of the Dutch government’s plans to cut waste.

The environmental standards inspectorate ILT estimates that up to 50 million illegally imported bottles are sold every year, often in restaurants and cafés that buy them from illegal traders.

In an echo of the Netherlands’ cannabis policy, importing canned drinks is outlawed, but buying and selling them after they cross the border is not, making the drinks attractive to outlets that want to avoid the cost and logistical burden of recycling thousands of cans.

Soft drinks are bought from Germany and Denmark, while beer is more commonly imported from Poland, all countries in the border-free Schengen zone.

The result is that the cans end up in landfill or as litter, hampering the government’s efforts to meet its recycling targets.

“It’s an illegal trade,” ILT acting inspector-general Edwin van Houten told EenVandaag. “They come into contact with organised crime because there is a huge amount of money to be earned from avoiding the rules. It runs into the millions of euros.”

Van Houten said the rules were difficult to enforce because only importation is illegal. In the last year 500 inspections were carried out and 90 companies were given warnings, but only five were fined.

“It’s a drop in the ocean and it costs a lot of capacity because we need to do far-reaching, deep investigations,” he said.

World.title: Parents of euthanasia teen go to court over prosecution letter
World.content:
The parents of a 17-year-old girl who chose to die by euthanasia in 2023 due to incurable psychological suffering have gone to court to force public prosecutors to identify a group of doctors that wrote a damning letter about the case.

Their daughter Milou’s psychological struggles were documented in a 2023 documentary, which covered her wish to be granted the right to voluntary death and the aftermath that followed.

The case caused significant public controversy and a group of 14 doctors subsequently wrote a letter suggesting a criminal investigation should be launched against the parents and doctors involved in treating her.

They called on prosecutors to find out “to what extent those close to this vulnerable patient (…) influenced this young patient’s decision to choose euthanasia.” The writers of the letter did not know Milou or her personal background and had not spoken to her themselves.

Eight of the signatories of the letter are still unnamed. In a courtroom in The Hague on Tuesday, the mother of Milou recounted how that letter had led to daily threats and intimidation, requiring the police to guard their home.

“As a parent, losing your child and having to miss them forever is the worst thing that can happen to you,” the mother Mireille Verhoof told the court. “Being accused afterwards of inciting the death of your child or being complicit in her death is beyond description and unbearable.”

She also said her daughter had effectively been “abused” by anti-euthanasia campaigners, who dismissed their integrity to further a political agenda.

The family’s lawyer Richard Korver also said that the people behind the letter should not be able to use their professional authority to make serious accusations and at the same time claim anonymity, reported to Omroep Brabant.

The public prosecution department still does not want to release the names so as to avoid further conflict and ensure people can bring judicial complaints in confidence. It also disputes that the letter was meant as a formal request for criminal proceedings.

The federation of doctors KNMG also condemned the letter, describing it as “indecent and unacceptable.” The court’s decision on the release of the names is expected on September 3.

If you or someone close to you is struggling with thoughts of suicide, help is available. In the Netherlands, call 113 or 0800-0113 (free) for 24/7 support, or visit 113.nl, where the chat service is available in English.

World.title: Dutch shops to stock more GM food after EU relaxes rules in 2028
World.content:
More genetically modified food is likely to appear in Dutch stores when rules on licensing and labelling are relaxed in two years’ time.

The European parliament passed a law before the summer recess allowing food retailers to stock products containing GM ingredients without labelling them as such, as long as they account for less than 1% of the contents.

The more flexible law was brought in to offset the effect of stricter limits on pesticides, which the EU wanted to halve by 2030, so that growers could use genetic modification to make their crops more resistant to parasites.

But two years ago the EU dropped the pesticides bill, which commission president Ursula von der Leyen said had become “a symbol of polarisation”, while still going ahead with the relaxation of GM rules.

Food products that have been significantly changed by genetic modification will still have to be licensed and labelled under the current rules.

Michelle Habets, a researcher at the Rathenau Institute, a science and technology think tank based in The Hague, said the more flexible rules risked undermining public confidence in supermarkets and other food retailers.

She told NOS she had spoken to dozens of consumers about the new law while it was passing through the European parliament. “Everyone agreed that genetically modified crops should be labelled,” she said.

“People admitted they don’t always study every label in the supermarket, but they think transparency is important, as is the freedom of choice for people who don’t want to eat those crops for whatever reason.”

Jeroen Candel, associate professor of food and agricultural policy at Wageningen University, said GM crops could bring benefits by reducing the need for pesticides, but added a note of caution.

“The new law is based on the idead that we can optimalise the current system of agriculture with new technology,” he said. “But if we do that, we are maintaining a system that is not sustainable in terms of climate and biodiversity.”

We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s government has unveiled plans to reduce income tax rates for an estimated 3.5 million people earning around or slightly above average salaries. The costs of the cuts would be covered by increasing the tax rate for large companies and individuals with the highest earnings. The changes, which Prime Minister Donald Tusk says are intended to “provide relief and assistance to the growing middle class”, would come into effect from next year – when the government is facing re-election. However, the proposals still require approval from parliament, where Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, has a majority, and President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and has vetoed a record number of bills. 📊 Nowa skala PIT będzie lepiej dopasowana do rosnących wynagrodzeń. Do 130 tys. zł pozostaje stawka 12%, między 130 a 150 tys. zł pojawi się 24%, a 32% zacznie obowiązywać dopiero powyżej 150 tys. zł. 💰 #WięcejWPortfelu pic.twitter.com/1S2MpSkVoC — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) August 19, 2026 The main elements of the proposed changes, which were outlined by Tusk and finance minister Andrzej Domański on Wednesday, are an increase in the earnings threshold at which the lowest rate of income tax is paid and the introduction of a new rate between the lowest and highest earnings brackets. Currently, there are two income tax brackets: the first taxes earnings of up to 120,000 zloty (around €27,800) at a rate of 12%; the second taxes earnings above that level at a rate of 32%. There is also a tax-free allowance for earnings of up to 30,000 zloty. Meanwhile, anyone who earns more than 1 million zloty a year pays an additional “solidarity levy” (effectively a third tax bracket) of 4% on income above that amount. Under the new proposals, the threshold for the first 12% tax bracket would be raised to 130,000 zloty. For earnings between 130,000 and 150,000 zloty, a new tax bracket of 24% would be introduced. Then earnings above 150,000 would be taxed at 32%. Tusk noted that, since his government took office, wages in Poland have increased by around 30%, bringing increasing numbers of people into the higher tax bracket. According to figures from Statistics Poland (GUS), a state agency, in June this year, average monthly earnings at companies employing more than nine people were 9,401.58 zloty, the equivalent of almost 113,000 zloty a year. “We’re not talking about millionaires here; we’re talking about a growing middle class…on whose shoulders the financing of state security, defence spending, etc. rests to a large extent,” said Domański. “We want to change this…so that those who work hard to earn their average wage can clearly feel the relief,” added Tusk. “And we want this to be financed by the wealthiest companies and the wealthiest individuals, who have the lowest tax burden.” The number of ultra-wealthy individuals in Poland has more than doubled since 2021, a faster rate of growth than anywhere else in the world, according to a new study https://t.co/MNKgmjzn2U — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 11, 2026 Therefore, in order to finance the middle-class tax cuts, Tusk and Domański announced that the government would seek to increase corporate income tax from 19% to 22% for firms and tax capital groups that generate annual revenues above €50 million. Meanwhile, the solidarity levy for individuals earning over 1 million zloty a year would be increased by one percentage point, to 5%. “I am absolutely convinced that this will make our tax system more equitable,” declared Tusk. However, he also conceded that raising the income-tax-free amount from 30,000 to 60,000 zloty – as his Civic Platform (KO) party promised to do within its first 100 days in office – would not be possible for budgetary reasons, in particular the need to finance high defence spending. Poland has introduced a new type of account that will allow individuals to invest up to 100,000 zloty (€23,200) tax free. The government says the scheme is designed to encourage Poles to build savings and channel money into the domestic financial market https://t.co/1xDHHJGYKX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 14, 2026 The prime minister said that the planned tax changes would be discussed further this week at a cabinet meeting devoted to next year’s state budget, which is currently being prepared. The relevant legislation will subsequently be submitted to parliament, with the aim of bringing it into force in 2027. However, Tusk acknowledged that there is a strong possibility of a veto by Nawrocki, who has blocked dozens of government bills, including fiscal measures. In December, Nawrocki vetoed an increase in the tax on alcoholic and sweet drinks. Last month, he effectively blocked a windfall tax on fuel companies’ excess profits by sending it to the constitutional court for review. However, he did approve a law increasing the corporate income tax rate for banks. President @NawrockiKn has obstructed a planned windfall tax on fuel companies by sending it to the constitutional court, where it could stay for years The tax aimed to offset fuel price protection costs after the Iran war surgehttps://t.co/UojVuYhvdV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 27, 2026 Next year’s budget will be closely watched given that Poland’s fiscal situation has become increasingly problematic in recent years. In 2024, the European Union placed Poland under its excessive deficit procedure, requiring Warsaw to commit to measures to bring down the deficit. However, last year the deficit actually rose, from 6.4% of GDP in 2024 to 7.3% in 2025, which was the second-highest level among all EU member states. This year, Poland’s public debt passed the EU’s limit of 60% of GDP for the first time on record. The situation has led two of the big three rating agencies, Fitch and Moody’s, to shift Poland’s credit outlook to negative. This year, Fitch warned that the political gridlock between Nawrocki and the government was making tackling the deficit and debt more difficult. Given that Poland will hold parliamentary elections in autumn 2027, it is unlikely that either the government or Nawrocki – who will be supporting the right-wing opposition – will be keen on any fiscal measures that either raise taxes or reduce spending in areas such as social policy and defence. Poland has launched a new advertising campaign to promote itself internationally and attract more tourists from “key European markets” and the United States. The new initiative, which has the slogan “Poland. More than you expected”, features global Polish icons such as football star Robert Lewandowski, supermodel Anja Rubik, and Hollywood filmmaker Jesse Eisenberg, who received Polish citizenship last year. A series of videos, the first of which was released Tuesday, will aim to present Poland as “modern, safe, diverse and authentic”, as well as “defying stereotypes”, says sports and tourism minister Jakub Rutnicki. Commissioned by his ministry and launched by the Polish Tourism Organisation (POT), the campaign will be conducted in Germany, Spain, Italy, the United Kingdom and the United States. The first video promotes Warsaw, Poland’s capital, and features Lewandowski, Rubik and Eisenberg appearing near the city’s landmarks. Polish actor Nikodem Rozbicki, meanwhile, plays the role of renowned 19th-century Polish composer Fryderyk Chopin. In the 30-second spot, Chopin’s character declares that Warsaw is “where my heart is” – a reference to the fact that Chopin’s heart, preserved in cognac, was brought back to the city from Paris by his sister shortly after his death in 1849 and is now immured in a pillar in the city’s Holy Cross Church. Lewandowski, who recently joined US football team Chicago Fire, tells viewers that Poland offers “more than you expected”, a reference to the campaign’s main slogan, which suggests to viewers that Poland may surprise them positively. “Research shows that people who have visited Poland rate it much more favourably than their previous perceptions or media reports suggested,” notes POT in its press release. Magdalena Krucz, the head of POT, adds that she believes the campaign “will be as surprising to audiences as Poland itself is to tourists who come to us for the first time”. However, the slogan is not new: it has been used by POT to promote Poland since 2021. The new campaign will also feature Nobel Peace Prize winner and former president Lech Wałęsa, who led the Solidarity movement that brought down Poland’s former communist regime. POT notes that he remains “one of the most recognisable symbols in the world of the fight for freedom and democracy”. The music is arranged by Radzimir Dębski, better known as Jimek, a Polish composer and conductor who has regularly performed with US rap legend Snoop Dogg. Polish-American NBA star @JeremySochan has joined a campaign to promote Poland as a tourist destination. His appearance has been received positively, but Sochan responded directly to one commentator who said a black person shouldn't be advertising Poland https://t.co/KXDok7IAXP — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 15, 2024 Poland has experienced a tourism boom in recent years. Last year, the country recorded the European Union’s second-fastest growth in the number of nights spent in tourist accommodation, behind only Malta. The biggest tourist draw is the historic city of Kraków, which was last year named the best city break destination in Europe by members of British consumer association and magazine Which? for the fifth time. This year, Time Out magazine rated Kraków the 16th best city in the world. However, the country has a wide range of tourist-friendly destinations, including long, sandy beaches on the northern Baltic coast, mountains in the south, the lake district of Masuria, as well as many historic cities and modern museums and galleries. Poland saw the EU's second-fastest growth in tourism in 2025, behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta https://t.co/WVkRbHtU7o — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 19, 2026 The city of Lublin in eastern Poland, which will be a European City of Culture in 2029, last year welcomed a record 2.2 million visitors, including over half a million from abroad. The city is known for its rich Jewish history, and featured prominently in the 2024 Oscar-nominated film A Real Pain, directed by and starring Eisenberg, whose ancestors were Jews from Lublin and the nearby town of Krasnystaw. Last year, the sport and tourism ministry announced that it wants tourism to contribute 9% of GDP within a decade, from about 5% now. The strategy includes creating a “Polish brand” through which internationally recognised athletes, artists, historical figures and products are showcased more prominently. Last month, the government appointed a marketing and branding expert to develop a unified strategy for promoting the country abroad, saying the move will help boost tourism, support Polish products and attract foreign investment. The city of Lublin in eastern Poland welcomed a record 2.2 million visitors in 2025. That included 506,000 from abroad, which was also the highest ever figure, with Brits, Israelis and Americans the most common foreign visitors https://t.co/6yMrRcf6ml — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 28, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Warsaw Uprising veteran and activist Wanda Traczyk-Stawska dies aged 99
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Wanda Traczyk-Stawska, a veteran of the Warsaw Uprising against Nazi-German occupation during World War Two, has died aged 99. Traczyk-Stawska, who survived imprisonment in German camps after the uprising, in her later years became a vocal advocate for the rights of women and disabled people. “Warsaw has lost someone extraordinary,” wrote Warsaw’s mayor, Rafał Trzaskowski, announcing her death on Wednesday. “A heroine, a soldier…but above all a teacher who, throughout her life, taught us what matters most: courage, dignity, and responsibility for our fellow human beings.” Odeszła Pani Wanda. Trudno w to uwierzyć. Warszawa straciła kogoś wyjątkowego – Bohaterkę, żołnierkę Powstania Warszawskiego, Honorową Obywatelkę miasta. Ale przede wszystkim nauczycielkę, która przez całe życie uczyła nas tego, co najważniejsze: odwagi, godności i… pic.twitter.com/uSNcsZ7c1P — Rafał Trzaskowski (@trzaskowski_) August 19, 2026 Traczyk-Stawska, born in Warsaw in 1927, was only 12 years old when Nazi Germany invaded Poland. She initially became involved in the Grey Ranks (Szare Szeregi), an underground resistance movement associated with the Polish scouting movement, participating in sabotage operations. She later joined the Home Army (AK), Poland’s main resistance force, and, at the age of 17, served as a riflewoman and liaison during the Warsaw Uprising, taking the nom de guerre “Pączek” (meaning “Bud”). Traczyk-Stawska was seriously injured while fighting in the uprising. After the revolt was defeated, she was taken prisoner and subsequently held in various prisoner-of-war camps in Germany until the end of the war. After returning to Poland, Traczyk-Stawska earned a degree in psychology and began working as a teacher of disabled children in Warsaw. At the same time, she became an active figure in commemorating the uprising and its participants. In her final years, Traczyk-Stawska also became politically active. In 2018, she visited parliament to support a protest by disabled people and their carers, who were seeking more state support. Two years later, at the age of 93, she and another female uprising veteran, Hanna Stadnik, joined the mass Women’s Strike protests that broke out in response to the introduction of a near-total ban on abortion under the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government. “We women will not relent this time,” she told broadcaster TVN at the time. “In the uprising, we fought for our freedom, because there is no dignity without freedom. If we are currently treated like incubators, we have the right to fight for our dignity…We will fight – unarmed, but to the last woman – not to be treated like objects.” Traczyk-Stawska was also among a group of female Uprising veterans who that year criticised PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński for wearing, during a speech condemning the Women’s Strike protests, a badge featuring the anchor symbol that was used by the Home Army during the war. She was also an advocate for women’s rights more broadly. In 2023, in a speech at the 79th anniversary of the uprising, Traczyk-Stawska noted that, “at the beginning, the generals shouted: ‘Why do we need so many women?'” But, by the time the uprising ended, “we had been given the same rights as boys. And we won’t get rid of these rights. Because everyone, whether a man or a woman, is a citizen of this country and has equality written into the constitution”. Her speech then became overtly political, saying that “this [PiS] government needs to be completely changed, as it doesn’t remember that women have their own position enshrined in the constitution. That we are equal to men.” In both the 2020 and 2025 presidential elections, Traczyk-Stawska expressed support for the candidacy of Trzaskowski, who is a deputy leader of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party that is PiS’s main opponent. However, in both elections, Trzaskowski lost to PiS-backed candidates. Odeszła Wanda Traczyk-Stawska ps. „Pączek” – Bohaterka, Patriotka, wzór odwagi i niezłomności. Pokazywała, że prawdziwy patriotyzm to budowanie wspólnoty, empatia i otwartość na świat. Cześć Jej pamięci! 🕯️🤍 Najgłębsze wyrazy współczucia dla Bliskich. pic.twitter.com/nY0ijDSBlJ — Monika Sikora ⚡️ (@Moni_Sikora) August 19, 2026 Following news of Traczyk-Stawska’s death, many prominent figures paid tribute to her, in particular from the current KO-led ruling coalition. “Farewell, heroine,” wrote KO leader and Prime Minister Donald Tusk, sharing a photo of himself with Traczyk-Stawska and quoting one of her statements: “Do not stand, do not watch when evil happens, but react immediately, for that is your duty.” While she had fought against German occupation, Traczyk-Stawska later called for reconciliation. In her 2023 speech, she called Germany “our best neighbour” and said that the two countries must now “stand together”, including supporting Ukraine against Russian aggression. Today, Germany’s ambassador to Poland, Miguel Berger, expressed his “great sadness” at Traczyk-Stawska’s death, calling her an “advocate of dialogue in the process of Polish-German reconciliation and a passionate champion of peace, freedom, and human dignity”. „Nie stój, nie patrz, gdy się zło dzieje, tylko reaguj natychmiast, bo to jest twój obowiązek." – Wanda Traczyk-Stawska Żegnaj, Bohaterko. pic.twitter.com/MhfqlszVcI — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) August 19, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland “99% sure” fugitive opposition politician is in pro-Russian breakaway region of Moldova
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, says that they are “99% certain” that fugitive opposition politician Marcin Romanowski is in Transnistria, a breakaway region of Moldova that has close links to Russia. Last week, judicial authorities in Poland confirmed that they had received a letter purportedly from Romanowski, who is wanted in Poland for 11 alleged crimes committed while he served as a deputy justice minister in the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government. In the document, Romanowski claimed to be in Transnistria and requested safe passage back to Poland. However, as the authenticity of the letter had not been confirmed, some media outlets speculated that the politician may not, in fact, be in Transnistria. Meanwhile, the Moldovan authorities quickly announced that they had no record of Romanowski travelling to Transnistria, which is a landlocked territory that only has borders with Moldova and Ukraine and operates no commercial passenger flights. A former government minister who fled criminal charges in Poland appears to be in Transnistria, a breakaway region of Moldova that has close links with Russia. Marcin Romanowski's whereabouts have been unknown since he left Hungary earlier this year https://t.co/MPWroFVbMe — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 13, 2026 Speaking on Tuesday morning, Przemysław Nowak, spokesman for Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office, said they have “still not confirmed” the veracity of Romanowski’s claim to be in Transnistria, reported broadcaster RMF. However, shortly afterwards, speaking ahead of a meeting of his cabinet on Tuesday, Tusk said he wanted to address the issue given there has been “a great deal of speculation and misinformation regarding Mr Romanowski and his whereabouts”. “I can say that the intelligence services of other countries in the region with which we cooperate have confirmed to us the information that Mr Romanowski is 99% certain – I say that just in case – to be in Transnistria, in Tiraspol,” he continued, referring to the capital of the breakaway region. "Pan Romanowski znajduje się na 99 procent w Naddniestrzu. Chyba nie trzeba tu komentarzy" Donald Tusk podczas posiedzenia rządu ⤵️ pic.twitter.com/muVQVKrOTs — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) August 18, 2026 Transnistria is a narrow strip of land in eastern Moldova that sought to become a separate state in the early 1990s as the Soviet Union collapsed, fighting a war between 1990 and 1992. Today, the territory, which has a population of around 360,000, operates as a de facto state but is not recognised by any other country. Its flag and national emblem feature the Soviet hammer and sickle. Transnistria has close ties with Russia, which maintains a military “peacekeeping” force there. Various experts and former intelligence officials have noted that it would be impossible for Romanowski to enter without Russia’s approval. The fact that Romanowski appears to be hiding there has led to criticism of PiS, the party Romanowski still technically serves as an MP and which publicly takes a strongly anti-Russian position. “If it is true that [Romanowski] is in Transnistria, a republic not recognised by anyone, de facto controlled 100% by Russia, then it must have happened through and with the participation of Russia,” said defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz last week. “Escaping under the Russian umbrella is the worst possible thing, because not only are they cowardly, but they are also joining the enemy of Poland,” he added. In his remarks today, Tusk said that Romanowski’s likely presence in Transnistria “speaks for itself regarding not only Mr Romanowski but the entire political group that covered up for and benefited from such people, and continues to cover up for them”. PiS politicians have largely avoided commenting, noting that it has not been confirmed that Romanowski is in Transnistria. However, deputy leader Przemysław Czarnek last week admitted that, if Romanowski did trael there, he would have “crossed a line”. Nie wyprzedzajmy faktów – powiedział poseł PiS Zbigniew Kuźmiuk, pytany, czy Marcin Romanowski może zostać zawieszony w partii.https://t.co/IQzuS8Ad7O — tvn24 (@tvn24) August 14, 2026 Romanowski served as a deputy justice minister in the former PiS government from 2019 until 2023, when the party lost power to a new ruling coalition led by Tusk. In 2024, prosecutors announced that they wanted to charge him with 11 crimes, including participating in an organised criminal group and using crime as a source of income. However, he instead fled to Hungary, where he was granted asylum by the then-government of Viktor Orbán, a PiS ally. When Orbán lost power earlier this year, his successor, Péter Magyar, promised to extradite both Romanowski and Zbigniew Ziobro, the former PiS justice minister who had also fled criminal charges in Poland and been granted asylum by Orbán. However, as Magyar was sworn in as the new prime minister, Ziobro fled to the United States, where he remains, and Romanowski disappeared, leading to months of speculation as to his whereabouts. Both politicians deny the accusations against them and claim to be victims of political persecution by Tusk’s government. Poland has formally asked the US to detain and extradite former justice minister @ZiobroPL, who faces multiple criminal charges. He denies wrongdoing and calls the case political revengehttps://t.co/BXdQgWm61q — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 27, 2026 In his comments on Tuesday morning, Nowak said that prosecutors had found “no grounds whatsoever” to approve Romanowski’s request for safe passage to Poland. He noted that “the suspect has evaded legal proceedings, questioned the legality of the authorities’ actions, left Poland and then Hungary to avoid arrest, and publicly declared his lack of intention to return to the country due to the ongoing criminal proceedings against him”. Polish prosecutors are still, however, attempting to confirm Romanowski’s whereabouts and secure his extradition to Poland to face justice. He is subject to a European Arrest Warrant. However, that applies only in EU countries, and Moldova is not a member of the bloc. World.title: FedEx-led €7.8bn takeover of Polish delivery giant InPost wins EU approval
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The European Commission has granted approval for a consortium led by American transportation conglomerate FedEx to take over Polish delivery giant InPost in a deal worth €7.8 billion (33.7 billion zloty). InPost, which operates in France, Spain, the UK, Portugal, Italy and the Benelux countries, as well as in its home market, confirmed on Tuesday that it had received the green light from the EU for the deal, which was announced in February. If it goes through, the takeover will see a consortium made up of FedEx along with existing InPost investors, Advent, A&R, and PPF, purchase all of the company’s shares at a price of €15.60 each. Konsorcjum inwestorów, w którym jednym z uczestników jest amerykański @FedEx, uzyskało bezwarunkową zgodę KE na nabycie wszystkich akcji @InPostPL @RBrzoska https://t.co/F4AleTCViO — WNP.PL (@wnppl) August 18, 2026 The group behind the deal says the aim is to help InPost continue its recent rapid expansion. The firm will retain its name, branding and Polish headquarters. Founder and CEO Rafał Brzoska will remain in place, as well as being a major shareholder through A&R, which is his investment vehicle. The deal will see Advent, an American private equity firm, and FedEx each hold 37% of InPost. A&R would have 16% and PPF, a Czech investment fund founded by the late billionaire Petr Kellner, 10%. Currently, PPF holds 28.75%, A&R 12.49%, and Advent 6.5%. The initial offer period for the consortium’s takeover was due to end on 27 July. However, on 22 July, it was extended until 18 September due to the fact that antitrust proceedings in the EU and Vietnam were still ongoing. In its announcement today of EU approval, InPost noted that it is still awaiting a green light from the Vietnam Competition Commission but expects a decision to be made by 8 September. Although the Polish company has no operations in Vietnam, FedEx has been present on the market since 1994. InPost has grown rapidly in recent years through its pioneering use of parcel lockers, first in Poland and then across western Europe. In the UK, it has established a network of over 14,000 parcel lockers, including in branches of the British Post Office. In June this year, French President Emannuel Macron thanked InPost for its latest investment in France, where the firm – which operates there through its subsidiary Mondial Relay – is planning to spend a further €500 million to expand its presence. In the first quarter of 2026, InPost saw its revenue rise 31% year-on-year to reach 3.9 billion zloty. That included 121% growth in the UK, 28% in the Eurozone and 9% in Poland itself. However, the group’s earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortisation (EBITDA), a measure of profitability of business operations, were down 4% to 902 million zloty. World.title: Twelve killed as Polish coach crashes in Hungary
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Twelve people have died after a bus carrying Polish pilgrims from Medjugorje in Bosnia and Herzegovina back to Poland crashed on a motorway in Hungary. Initial findings indicate that the cause of the accident was the driver of the coach falling asleep. Political leaders in both Poland and Hungary have offered condolences to the families of the victims, while the Polish foreign ministry has set up a special helpline for those affected. BREAKING: 12 people have been killed after a Polish tourist bus crashed on a motorway in Hungary https://t.co/PAiZ4D1jU3 📺 Sky 501, Virgin 602, Freeview 233 and YouTube pic.twitter.com/yxW9tBN5bw — Sky News (@SkyNews) August 16, 2026 The accident occurred at around 1 a.m. local time on the night of Saturday to Sunday on the M3 motorway in Hungary. Later on Sunday morning, Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar confirmed that 12 people had died and at least 10 were seriously injured. According to information from the Hungarian emergency services, 57 passengers and two drivers had been on the bus. “The driver probably fell asleep at the wheel”, resulting in the vehicle veering off the road and into a ditch, said police in a statement quoted by Polsat News. Polsat reports that the group is from around Strzyżów, a town in southeastern Poland. The owner of the local company that had been transporting them told Business Insider Polska that the coach “was driven by two experienced drivers”. Twelve people lost their lives and at least ten were seriously injured overnight when a bus carrying Polish tourists overturned and went off the road into a ditch on the M3 motorway. My sincere condolences to the families of the victims. I am grateful to all those who took part… — Magyar Péter (Ne féljetek) (@magyarpeterMP) August 16, 2026 Polish media outlets reported that the group in the bus were pilgrims on their way back to Poland from Medjugorje, which is a popular destination for Catholic pilgrimages due to a series of reported visions of the Virgin Mary that have occurred there. Polish foreign ministry spokesman Maciej Wewiór later confirmed to broadcaster TVN that “everything indicates they were returning from Medjugorje”. The authorities in Podkarpackie, the province of Poland where the group was from, also reported that they were pilgrims returning from Bosnia and Herzegovina. The accident on Sunday morning took place just after the end of celebrations of the Assumption of Mary on Saturday, which had included the unveiling in Poland of Europe’s tallest statue of Mary. Poland’s president, Karol Nawrocki, issued a statement on Sunday morning expressing his “deep sorrow…in the face of this unimaginable tragedy” and offering “prayer and profound compassion for the families and loved ones of the victims”. Prime Minister Donald Tusk likewise expressed his “deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of the victims” and thanked the Hungarian emergency services for undertaking the rescue operation. Andrii Sybiha, the foreign minister of Ukraine, which borders both Poland and Hungary, also offered his “heartfelt condolences” and said that “Ukraine stands in solidarity with the friendly Polish people and shares their grief”. The Polish embassy in Budapest has set up a special helpline for family members and loved ones of those involved in the crash. World.title: Europe’s biggest Virgin Mary statue – taller than Rio’s Christ the Redeemer – unveiled in Polish village
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The tallest statue of the Virgin Mary in Europe has been officially opened in the small village of Konotopie in central Poland. Towering over the rural landscape at 55.6 metres high, the monument, whose construction was funded by a wealthy local couple, is taller than the famous Christ the Redeemer statue in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. The new landmark, which is also the tallest religious statue of any kind in Europe, was unveiled on 15 August, when Catholics celebrate the assumption of Mary into heaven. The consecration ceremony was led by Krzysztof Wętkowski, bishop of the diocese of Włocławek in which Konotopie, which has a population of only around 130 people, is located. The local community hopes that the statue will become a major site of pilgrimage. Among those to attend the ceremony was former Polish president and Nobel Peace Prize winner Lech Wałęsa. “We sinners ask Our Lady of Mercy to take care of the whole nation,” wrote the 82-year-old in a post on social media, sharing photos of himself at the statue. Construction of the concrete statue took 18 months and reportedly cost around 100 million zloty (€23.2 million). Those costs were covered by the couple behind the project, Roman and Grażyna Karkosik. After making his fortune investing in undervalued companies during Poland’s post-communist transition in the 1990s, Roman Karkosik had by the early 21st century become one of Poland’s richest people, though his fortune has since diminished somewhat, according to estimates. The couple – who keep an extremely low profile, rarely giving interviews and never speaking publicly about the project to build the statue of Mary – live in a restored 18th-century palace around 2 kilometres away, from where they can see the new monument. Konotopie’s statue of Mary has now overtaken one in Miribel, France, as Europe’s tallest. But it is still some distance behind the tallest in the world, the 98-metre Mother of All Asia–Tower of Peace in Batangas City, Philippines. Until recently, Poland also had the tallest statue of Jesus in the world, the 33-metre-high Jesus Christ the King of the Universe monument, erected in the town of Świebodzin in 2010. However, in 2024, it was overtaken by a 61-metre-tall statue of Jesus in Indonesia. The design for the statue of Mary in Konotopie was originally conceived in the form of a two-metre-high model by sculptor Adam Jakub Matejkowski, who told the Polish edition of Forbes magazine that the Karkosiks had specifically requested that the statue be larger than Świebodzin’s Christ. Chief engineer Bartłomiej Niesłuchowski told broadcaster TVN that it took months to find a company willing and able to undertake such a project. Because no suppliers in Poland could produce the material needed for the unique mould into which the concrete would be poured, it had to be manufactured in Italy. The monument will be free for the public to access, including its observation deck, located 15 metres up on the pedestal upon which Mary stands. The site is expected to become a place of pilgrimage, with local authorities preparing for an influx of people. “We’re already seeing growing interest in investment plots, including restaurants,” Renata Gołębiewska, mayor of the nearby town of Kikoł, told the Rzeczpospolita daily. “But it’s too early to assess the impact.” Poland is one of Europe’s most religious countries. Just over 70% of the population identify as Catholic, according to the most recent national census, while around 30% attend Sunday mass. However, religiosity has been falling rapidly in recent years, especially among young Poles. The Catholic church in Poland has also been hit by a series of scandals relating to historical child sex abuse as well as accusations that it interferes in politics. The proportion of Catholics who attend Sunday mass in Poland has stabilised at around 30% after falling from a peak of 57%, new church data show. The proportion of children taking Catholic catechism in schools has continued to fall but remains a majority https://t.co/5bu35hzJ7c — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 17, 2025 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish opposition expels 40 lawmakers who formed breakaway caucus led by ex-PM Morawiecki
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland’s largest opposition party, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), has expelled 40 of its lawmakers in response to them forming a breakaway parliamentary caucus led by PiS deputy leader and former prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki. The decision formalises a split that began last month, when Morawiecki and his supporters refused to resign from a political association they had formed and sign a pledge of loyalty to PiS. They represented a more moderate faction that had long been unhappy with the party’s move in a hard-right direction. Koleżeński Sąd Dyscyplinarny PiS podjął decyzję o wykluczeniu z partii 38 posłów i 2 senatorów wchodzących w skład klubu Rozwój Plus, w tym byłego premiera Mateusza Morawieckiego – przekazał rzecznik dyscyplinarny PiS Karol Karski. https://t.co/Qe6KuPVUVZ — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) August 13, 2026 On Thursday, PiS’s disciplinary spokesman, Karol Karski, announced that its disciplinary court had found that 38 MPs and two senators “seriously violated the PiS statute by leaving the PiS parliamentary caucus and joining a new caucus” founded by Morawiecki, called Development Plus (Rozwój Plus). Karski added that all 40, including Morawiecki, had been notified of the decision by email and been sent scans of the ruling. They have seven days to appeal. If no appeal is filed, they will officially cease to be PiS members, Karski said. A statement from the party’s disciplinary court, cited by news website Onet, also noted that Morawiecki had committed a further “serious violation” of the party’s statute by announcing last week that Development Plus would become a political party. Mateusz Morawiecki has confirmed that his Development Plus group, which is splitting from the national-conservative opposition PiS party, will soon form a party of its own. However, he categorically ruled out ever working with Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/J6mQaer4MA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 4, 2026 Among those to be expelled are several former government ministers, including Janusz Cieszyński, Paweł Jabłoński, Olga Semeniuk-Patkowska and Szymon Szynkowski vel Sęk. Some of the ousted lawmakers expressed their disappointment at PiS’s decision. “Someone who has done everything for PiS is being expelled simply because he wanted to broaden the party’s voter base,” Grzegorz Puda, another former minister, told the Fakt daily. Another, Łukasz Schreiber, told news website Onet that, in reality, the decision to expel them had been taken when party leader Jarosław Kaczyński said in July they had effectively resigned by refusing to sign the loyalty pledge. “Everything else was just a formality.” Morawiecki served as prime minister from 2017 until 2023, when PiS lost power to the current government, a more liberal coalition led by Donald Tusk. The party has plunged into crisis this year, with its support in polls falling to the lowest level in over 15 years. In response to a growing challenge from the far right, Kaczyński has shifted PiS itself rightwards. That frustrated more moderate figures around Morawiecki, who founded the Development Plus association in April this year as a way of promoting their ideas. However, that prompted criticism from some other members of the party, who saw it as a step towards creating a breakaway group. The split in PiS is a blow to the party and its leader, Jarosław Kaczyński. But the potential emergence of a new centre-right party led by Mateusz Morawiecki could actually help the opposition win a majority at next year's elections, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/xMP7e4rOFf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 31, 2026 Matters came to a head in July, when Morawiecki and his supporters refused to quit their association and sign the pledge of loyalty demanded by Kaczyński. They then formed their own caucus, which immediately became the third largest in parliament and meant that PiS’s was no longer the biggest. Last week, Morawiecki confirmed that his group would soon form a new party of its own. He laid out a vision of a more moderate, centre-right party that would focus on economic development rather than “ideological disputes”. Its first policy proposal was to establish a special “salary” for parents, equivalent to the minimum wage, that they would be paid for the first three years of a child’s life, with the aim of boosting Poland’s birth rate, which is one of the lowest in the world. According to poll aggregator eWybory.eu, Development Plus already has average support of 5.6% in polls, despite not yet being a party. Support for PiS has fallen to 20.3%, down from 24.4% in July. World.title: Students in Czech Republic Face Higher Rents as Housing Costs Rise
World.content:
Students looking for private accommodation in Czech university cities this year are facing higher rents, with prices for some types of housing up by as much as 14 percent compared with 2025.

The increase comes as demand for student accommodation reaches its annual peak ahead of the winter semester.

Data from several Czech property platforms show that the busiest period started earlier this year, meaning students who have not yet found accommodation may face a more limited and expensive selection in September.

Those unable to secure a place in a student dormitory generally have three alternatives: renting a small apartment alone, taking a private room in a shared apartment, or renting a bed in shared accommodation.



The most expensive option is usually a small one-bedroom apartment with a kitchenette, typically around 30 square meters. According to the REMAX network, monthly rents for these apartments range from more than CZK 7,000 in Ústí nad Labem to around CZK 14,000 in Prague.

Prices have not increased evenly across the country. Brno recorded the sharpest rise, with rents for small apartments increasing by 12 percent year on year.

Prague saw a 4 percent increase, while rents in Hradec Králové and Pardubice rose by almost 9 percent. Olomouc was one of the few exceptions, with prices falling by slightly more than 2 percent.

Rent is not the only expense students need to consider. Utilities, water and maintenance charges can add another CZK 1,000 to CZK 2,000 a month, according to property platforms.

Private rooms offer a cheaper alternative

Many students instead rent individual rooms in shared apartments, with properties ranging from smaller 2+kk and 2+1 layouts to larger 4+kk and 4+1 apartments. Czech property portal Sreality.cz puts the average cost of a private room in university cities at between approximately CZK 5,700 in Opava and CZK 11,500 in Prague.

In Prague, private rooms listed on Sreality.cz were around 10 percent more expensive than during the same period last year. Prices in Brno, meanwhile, remained roughly unchanged.

Shared housing remains the cheapest option

For students on a tighter budget, sharing an apartment and renting a bed rather than an entire room remains the least expensive choice. The more people share a property, the lower the individual housing costs tend to be.

Even this option, however, has become more expensive. According to UlovDomov.cz, the cost of renting a bed has increased by several hundred Czech crowns compared with last year.

Prague remains considerably more expensive. A bed in a two-bedroom apartment costs almost CZK 5,500, about CZK 1,200 more than a bed in a three-bedroom apartment.

World.title: 58 Years Since Warsaw Pact Troops Invaded Czechoslovakia
World.content:
On August 21, 1968, Soviet troops and their Warsaw Pact allies invaded Czechoslovakia to bring an end to that country’s brief period of political liberalization, called the Prague Spring.

People still recall waking up on that fateful morning to find that Soviet-led Warsaw Pact tanks had rolled into the country, crushing all hope of implementing the democratic reforms of the Prague Spring. Shocked citizens took to the streets in protest of the invasion.

About 500,000 troops were involved in the invasion and occupation, during which 137 Czechoslovaks died and some 500 were wounded.

One of the key battles was for the control of Czech Radio, similar to the one that took place at the end of the Second World War.

The invasion ended the political and economic reforms led by Alexander Dubcek and reasserted dominant Soviet and Communist authority in Czechoslovakia.

It also helped establish the Brezhnev Doctrine, which Moscow said allowed the U.S.S.R. to intervene in any country where a communist government was under threat.

Within the following year, resistance faded, Dubček was removed from office, his reforms were undone, and a more Soviet-controlled government was installed.

World.title: Prague’s Groovy Market Fest Returns After a Successful Debut
World.content:
A new urban festival is aiming to become a regular fixture on Prague’s cultural calendar after attracting 1,200 visitors to its first edition in Riegrovy sady.

Groovy Market Fest, held on August 1, brought together food, design, music and local brands in a format inspired by European city markets.

According to the organizers, around 85% of visitors were tourists or foreign residents of Prague, highlighting the event’s appeal beyond the Czech-speaking audience.



The festival will return to Riegrovy sady on September 5, with further editions planned for October, November and December.

From Barcelona to Prague

Groovy Market Fest was founded by Marek Novák and Veronika Kracíková, a couple with experience in Prague’s food scene and Barcelona’s street-food culture.

Their interest in international gastronomy also led them to compete in Spain. In 2025, they won first place in the Cooking The Street competition, where their dish was judged by a professional panel that included chefs Beñat Ormaetxea and Jon Kepa Aurrecoetxea.

After returning to Prague, they decided to develop their own event, drawing inspiration from markets such as Barcelona’s Palo Alto Market.

The First Edition

Food Garden focused on gastronomy, while Palm Street featured local products and handmade goods. The Design Zone presented Czech brands working in fashion, design and art.

Rather than filling the site with as many vendors as possible, the organizers selected a smaller number of participants. They say the approach was intended to create a more coherent experience for visitors.

Music was another part of the programme, with live performances and DJ sets throughout the event. Visitors could also attend a masterclass focused on preparing the festival’s signature Groovy cocktail.

Additional editions are scheduled for October 3, November 7 and December 5, all at the same location.

Tickets for upcoming editions are available through GoOut.

World.title: Faster Than the Metro. New Bus is Now Linking Prague 8 and Prague 6
World.content:
A new bus service running through Prague’s Blanka tunnel has begun operating, offering a direct connection between the northern part of the city and Dejvice.

Bus line 145 connects Čimice and Kobylisy in Prague 8 with Hradčanská and Dejvická in Prague 6. The journey takes around 15 minutes, according to Prague’s public transport authority ROPID.



The same trip by metro requires a change between lines C and A in the city centre and takes around 22 minutes.

Including the time spent walking through stations and using escalators, the journey can take about half an hour.

The first day of operation brought mostly positive results, with many buses arriving on time or even ahead of schedule. The real test will come during regular weekday traffic, when congestion around Prague is heavier.

Where the new bus runs

In the direction from Čimice to Dejvice, line 145 serves:

Sídliště Čimice – Čimice – Libeňská – Řepínská – Podhajská pole – Čimický háj – Písečná – Služská – Kobylisy – Okrouhlická – Vychovatelna – Hradčanská – Vítězné náměstí – Dejvická

The return route follows the same corridor in the opposite direction.

The key feature of line 145 is its use of the Blanka tunnel, allowing buses to avoid the city centre and provide a direct connection between Prague 8 and Prague 6.

The new route is expected to make commuting easier for residents of Čimice, Kobylisy and surrounding neighbourhoods, while providing an alternative to the metro for journeys towards Dejvice and Hradčanská.

World.title: Leo Express to Launch Direct Prague–Brno Trains in December
World.content:
Leo Express is set to begin operating direct trains between Prague and Brno in December, marking the private carrier’s first direct connection between the two cities.

The company has already been serving passengers in the South Moravian Region, but its trains have so far bypassed Brno.

Over the past year, travellers from towns such as Hodonín and Břeclav have been able to use Leo Express services to reach Prague, travelling via Přerov and Olomouc.



The new Prague–Brno service will change that, putting the carrier directly on one of the Czech Republic’s busiest rail routes.

There is, however, one limitation for passengers travelling to Prague.

Leo Express trains do not serve Prague Main Station. In Prague, passengers must use Praha-Libeň station, which may be less convenient for those travelling to the city centre.

Leo Express was founded by businessman Leoš Novotný and has operated passenger trains in the Czech Republic since 2012.

The company has gradually expanded its network in the Czech Republic and abroad, competing with established operators such as České dráhy and RegioJet.

The Prague–Brno connection is expected to become another important part of the company’s Czech network from December.

World.title: Romanian Community to Celebrate Culture and Traditions in Prague
World.content:
The Romanian community in Czechia will come together in Prague on September 6 for the 12th edition of the Romanian Celebration, an annual event highlighting Romanian culture, traditions and the community’s ties with Czech society.

The main event will take place at the Ethnographic Section of the National Museum of the Czech Republic in Kinský Park, Prague 5.

The program will bring together Romanian music, dance, food, literature and activities for children.



Organized by the Association of Romanians in the Czech Republic (ARRC), the event is part of a wider cultural project running from March 1 to November 30, 2026.

Visitors can expect traditional music and dance performances, educational activities for children, cultural exhibitions, book presentations and Romanian gastronomy.

The event is aimed at members of the Romanian community, Romanian-speaking families, children and young people, as well as Czech residents interested in Romanian culture.

According to ARRC, the project aims to preserve and promote Romanian cultural and linguistic identity among Romanians living in the Czech Republic while creating opportunities for greater interaction between the Romanian and Czech communities.

“Through this project, we aim to offer the Romanian community, Romanian speakers, and lovers of the Romanian language a space for meeting, dialogue, and celebration of our cultural values, while also contributing to the consolidation of intercultural relations between Romania and the Czech Republic,” the ARRC leadership said.

World.title: Czech Fish Farmers Take Emergency Measures Amid Prolonged Drought
World.content:
Fish farmers reduce or suspend supplementary feeding to lower oxygen consumption, reports say.

Fish farmers in the Czech Republic have begun taking emergency measures as a prolonged drought, worsened by high temperatures across Europe, strains water supplies.

Facing water shortages, fish farmers have reduced or suspended supplementary feeding to lower fish oxygen consumption, while ponds are being regularly aerated, according to the report.



Several ponds have also been netted earlier than usual.

In the Třeboň area, which delivers tons of carp for the Czech Christmas table, part of the 200-hectare Koclířov pond has been drained and the fish moved to holding tanks.

More than a third of the water is missing from the region’s famous system of fish ponds due to the drought. The water level in Lake Svět, for example, has fallen by 98 centimetres. High temperatures are also causing water to evaporate more quickly.

The Czech government is expected to address the 2027 budget, upcoming elections and measures to tackle worsening drought.

Prime Minister Andrej Babiš has pledged an extra CZK 4 billion for drought-related measures. If approved, ministers will present plans for implementing them.

World.title: Burgermeister to Open First Prague Restaurant on Wenceslas Square in 2027
World.content:
Berlin burger chain Burgermeister is preparing to enter the Czech market, with its first Prague restaurant expected to open in early 2027.

The company has chosen Wenceslas Square for its debut. The location will also serve as a base for Burgermeister’s planned expansion across the Czech Republic, with more restaurants already in the pipeline.

Burgermeister has built its reputation in Berlin over the past two decades, growing from a single restaurant in a former public toilet into an international chain with 32 locations across Germany and other European markets.



Burgermeister has not yet revealed the exact address or confirmed a specific opening date.

The Prague restaurant will follow the concept that made Burgermeister popular in Berlin. The chain focuses on freshly prepared burgers and fries, with part of its food production handled in-house. Its operations also include its own bakery.

From a former public toilet to an international burger chain

Burgermeister opened its first restaurant in the Kreuzberg district of Berlin in 2006. The location was far from a conventional restaurant site. It occupied a former public toilet beneath the railway tracks near Schlesisches Tor station.

The unusual setting quickly became part of the brand’s identity. Over the years, Burgermeister expanded beyond its original Berlin location and developed into a larger restaurant chain.

Today, the company has 32 branches and is pursuing its goal of building a pan-European network.

World.title: PM Magyar’s first 100 days: Success or failure for Hungary?
World.content:
Péter Magyar’s first 100 days as Hungary’s prime minister have produced two sharply different verdicts. The Tisza government says it has already delivered more than 100 commitments and put the country on a new course, while Fidesz, now in opposition, argues that the period has been defined by broken election promises, improvisation and “Facebook government”. So what does the first 100 days actually tell us?

The milestone has particular political significance in Hungary. Magyar’s Tisza Party came to power after the April 2026 parliamentary election, ending 16 years of consecutive Fidesz-led governments. The new administration therefore inherited not only the state apparatus but expectations of a rapid and visible break with the previous era.

Péter Magyar’s first 100 days: government points to a new direction

Magyar’s central argument is that 100 days could never be enough to repair problems accumulated over a decade and a half, but were sufficient to change Hungary’s direction.

According to the Magyar government’s official assessment, more than 100 commitments have already been fulfilled. It highlights changes to the rule of law, anti-corruption measures, public media, government spending and the handling of state assets. The government has published its own assessment on its results website, inviting voters to check its pledges against what has been implemented.

One of the government’s most significant claims concerns EU funding. In May, Magyar announced an agreement with the European Commission concerning the release of EUR 16.4 billion – around HUF 6 trillion – in previously blocked European funds. Of this, EUR 4.4 billion was earmarked for cohesion programmes, with further sums intended for education, research, the electricity grid and new railway and HÉV suburban trains.

The government also points to a change in institutional practices. It allowed the special legal order used for decree-based government to expire after six years, while the former public media news operation was abolished in July and its leadership replaced. It has also established a National Asset Recovery and Protection Office as part of its anti-corruption agenda.

On public spending, the cabinet says it has tightened controls and reviewed large state investments. It claims savings of HUF 100 billion (around EUR 274 million) on the M6 motorway project and a further HUF 59 billion (EUR 162 million) on the Mohács bridge project.

Fidesz: major election promises remain unfulfilled

Fidesz offers an almost entirely opposite assessment.

In a statement issued on Wednesday, the opposition parliamentary group accused Magyar of winning the election with “false promises” and said the government had spent its first 100 days blaming its predecessor rather than delivering on its commitments.

Among the measures Fidesz says remain unfulfilled are the promised doubling of family allowance, maternity support, benefits for elderly people, GYES and GYET family benefits, a 25% pay rise for social-sector workers and a reduction of VAT on healthy food to 5%.

The party also attacked the government over the end of the interest-rate cap, its approach to the previous government’s Otthon Start housing programme and household energy subsidies. It further accused Tisza of favouring multinational companies over Hungarian businesses and of failing to deliver promises concerning fuel prices and medicine VAT. These are political allegations made in the Fidesz statement, which did not provide detailed evidence for each claim.

School support illustrates the broader dispute over delivery. Magyar has highlighted a HUF 100,000 (around EUR 274) back-to-school payment as one of his government’s social measures. During the campaign, however, Tisza said the scheme would help around 700,000 disadvantaged families, while the government’s current 100-day summary refers to assistance for around 400,000 disadvantaged children and families.

As we wrote yesterday about leaked information: Fidesz could be dismantled within weeks as its fate rests with members – and János Lázár

Success or failure? The answer depends on the benchmark

The two sides are measuring the same 100 days by different standards. Magyar emphasises structural change: relations with Brussels, institutional reforms, tighter spending controls and a break with several practices associated with the previous government. Fidesz focuses instead on household finances and campaign promises that voters could expect to feel directly.

That makes a simple success-or-failure verdict difficult. The first 100 days have brought clear changes in the machinery and direction of government, including a major agreement on EU funding. At the same time, several high-profile social commitments cited during the campaign have either not yet been implemented or remain politically disputed.

For Magyar, the larger test therefore begins after the symbolic 100-day mark. Whether the new direction translates into better healthcare, education, transport, economic growth and living standards will ultimately matter more than either side’s first political scorecard.
