Payments from two Australian scam victims were made to USC Market Place, an Israeli company that lists an employee of GoBe Marketing as its director.

New South Wales Mid North Coast resident Susan paid $378.50 to Finterex Capital, an unregulated trading platform that was later added to Australia's MoneySmart watchlist.

The ABC found Susan's contact details — and this exact payment – logged in the Sapphire Network's internal spreadsheets, along with those of another 4,000 Australian victims.

Susan was later refunded when she disputed the charge.

Two payments from another Australian victim named Anna also line up exactly with the scammers' internal spreadsheet. The fraudulent platform she interacted with, Ambit Capital, was named alongside her transactions.

When asked about Susan's payment, Goldberg texted back: "Sorry but I have no clue about any of this".

And yet, the Sapphire Network's internal documents contained another clue about his involvement.

Goldberg's fingerprints in the Sapphire Network

In a screen recording leaked from inside the Sapphire Network, a back-office worker is surveilled as they toil away in a spreadsheet.

The video shows an inside view of the scam network's money laundering operation, in which a payment processor called Smart Pay plays a starring role.

On one monitor, the worker pulls information from the Smart Pay dashboard.

A screenshot of a Sapphire Network staffer using the Smart Pay dashboard to log payments. (Supplied: OCCRP)

On their other screen they log payments in a similar spreadsheet to the ones where we found Anna's and Susan's payment details.

Later, the worker switches to an encrypted message thread titled "Smart pay — ScholarCloset", and continues their mind-numbing work of logging payments.

Several other videos in the leak connect this payment processor to Shefi Goldberg.

Smart Pay was integrated into the Sapphire Network’s payment processing infrastructure. (Supplied: OCCRP)

A spreadsheet of transactions is shared by an email address info@smart-pay.biz — the main email address of a company called Allegiant Holdings Ltd. That company previously traded as Smart Pay.

The same company name appears in another video, in which someone named Ronen demonstrates how to create payment invoices for $US250 each — the exact cost of the initial charge made to many scam victims.

Company records show that this company, Allegiant Holdings Ltd, is registered in Cyprus and is not to be confused with the unrelated Allegiant Holdings Ltd registered in the UK.

When first asked about Allegiant Holdings Ltd, Goldberg denied owning any entities in Cyprus. But the company registration documents tell a different story: Shefi Goldberg is the sole shareholder.

It's another link between Goldberg and the Sapphire Network, in addition to the scam payments made to three separate companies connected to his business.

Goldberg later said in a statement, "with respect to the Cypriot company, it is used for the provision of services. I am merely registered in connection with the company and am not involved in the management or day-to-day operation of its business."

It has been two years since Rodger was scammed by the Sapphire Network. He's moved on with his life, having given up on getting his money back.

But for Toby, the effects are still fresh. He is trying to make sense of the tricks that were played on him, the lies he was told and the half a million dollars he is unlikely to ever get back.

How we reported this story

World.title: Uber orders among accidental personal charges repaid by public servants
World.content:
Public servants have had to hand back hundreds of thousands of dollars in inadvertent personal charges, including food delivery orders, incurred on taxpayer-funded credit cards.

New figures provided to the Senate detail thousands of transactions in the past financial year where workers across multiple departments breached credit card rules.

At the Home Affairs Department, employees were required to repay 477 purchases made between July last year and March this year worth $28,400.

The accidental personal purchases included 149 transactions valued at about $5,500 that were related to Uber or Uber Eats.

A spokesperson for the department said all private expenditure must be repaid and it had processes to "support the appropriate use" of credit cards.

Katy Gallagher is confident the "system is working". (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

"Accidental personal expenditure can arise across a range of categories, for example purchases from restaurants, fast food and convenience stores as well as taxis," they said.

Public servants at the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade (DFAT) were also required to repay roughly $151,000 in personal charges last financial year.

The biggest of the 2,029 inadvertent transactions was worth more than $3,000, which was repaid in full.

A DFAT spokesperson noted its policies banned private expenditure on corporate credit cards and said any personal transaction charged in error must be repaid.

At the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet, workers had to reimburse 81 inadvertent purchases worth about $2,400, with most of them relating to Uber.

In a statement, Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said she had confidence in the processes in place to manage credit card usage in departments and agencies.

Pollies charge taxpayers $1.1m for family travel in 12 months Family reunion travel is under scrutiny as new analysis shows federal MPs and senators spent $1.1 million on flying and driving their loved ones to Canberra and around Australia in 12 months.

"The information presented shows that the system is working — in that inappropriate use is identified and paid back," she said.

"Agencies and secretaries are required to manage this appropriately at departmental level."

However, Deputy Opposition Leader Jane Hume said thousands of inappropriate transactions across government raised legitimate questions about whether existing controls were sufficiently effective.

"While it is encouraging that these purchases are identified and the vast majority repaid, the scale is concerning," she said.

AFP among agencies and departments misusing credit cards

The Australian Federal Police (AFP) also recorded 987 erroneous personal transactions on corporate credit cards last financial year valued at more than $42,000.

"Where inadvertent personal expenses are incurred, they must be repaid within one working day of the member becoming aware of the accidental use," an AFP spokesperson said.

Employees at the Health Department accumulated about $5,370 in accidental private purchases in the 2025-26 financial year.

A spokesperson for the department said it undertook compliance reviews and that cardholders cannot withdraw cash from their credit cards.

Labor puts squeeze on public service After it campaigned against a Coalition pledge to cut 41,000 public servants, Labor is ramping up its own efficiency drive.

The Department of Employment and Workplace Relations also recorded $8,688 in inadvertent personal purchases, with all of them repaid.

At the Department of Social Services, $2,250 in accidental personal purchases on work credit cards were paid back.

Both the employment and social services departments noted personal purchases were banned on work-issued credit cards.

The Department of Defence meanwhile recorded 3,276 purchases valued at about $240,000 that it described as "contrary to Defence policy".

The department has confirmed at least $213,672 of it has been paid back.

"Defence maintains a strong compliance and control framework to ensure inadvertent personal purchases are identified and addressed," a spokesperson said.

World.title: Tony reaches behind the bravado to a different Anthony Bourdain
World.content:
In his book Kitchen Confidential, Anthony Bourdain wrote these words: "I was — to be frank — a spoiled, miserable, narcissistic, self-destructive and thoughtless young lout, and badly in need of a good ass-kicking." Harsh, humbling words that somehow endear you to their subject, despite the warning label.

Fast facts about Tony What: The semi-true story of Anthony Bourdain's first time in a commercial kitchen. Starring: Dominic Sessa, Antonio Banderas, Emilia Jones, Leo Woodall. Directed by: Matt Johnson. When: In cinemas now. Likely to make you feel: Reflective, inspired, insouciant.

These words now mark the beginning of what its subject would refer to as a bildungsroman; of how "Tony" became the great chef and writer Anthony Bourdain. Tony, directed by Matt Johnson (Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie, BlackBerry) and starring Dominic Sessa (The Holdovers), is incredibly confident in its subject matter and visual language, and so convincing in its central thesis, which boils down to something like: "a good ass-kicking builds character", that it hardly needs the pretence.

Tony has an immediate look and feel to it that evokes a bygone time without being overly rose tinted, thanks to cinematography by Michael Bauman and lighting by Chris Hill. It's the 1970s, and we are about to see Anthony Bourdain's baptism by fire in his first ever kitchen job in Provincetown, Cape Cod. The food looks spectacular, the water is glistening, and the sky is as blue as can be, but this coming-of-age tale is not without its dark clouds and shadows.

A film based on a true story is not easy to nail and biopics, in particular, often crumble under the weight of reverence for their subject. So, it's refreshing that Tony does not shy away from showing the darker sides of the young Bourdain.

Dominic Sessa with director Matt Johnson on the set of Tony. (Supplied: A24)

Set during a short period of his life, when the 19-year-old's pursuit of a girl led to both gruelling hardship and untold opportunity, we see him try, and spectacularly fail, to achieve his dreams of being a writer. His wins are few, his mess-ups are innumerous, and his sardonic wit is less "rockstar TV host" and more "annoying brat". He corrects people's grammar, insists on using academic words in regular settings, and is so cocksure in his approach to women that he fails to notice (or wilfully ignores) when he's not wanted. The success of the flick hinges entirely on depicting Bourdain as a fallible, flawed character, without going so far as to lose audience empathy.

Good thing, then, that Dominic Sessa is more than up to the task. He may not be the spitting image of Bourdain, but his naturally lanky limbs and dark curls aid a portrayal that performs best when the actor says little to nothing at all. Sessa embodies that "thoughtless young lout" effortlessly, with a natural magnetism that makes him very easy to watch, and an old-school aura that lends itself to the 1970s very well.

Tony, a new film, takes in the early years of Anthony Bourdain's life. (Supplied: A24)

Though Anthony would later be known for his wordcraft, this young cad is not yet the Bourdain we know. Instead, Tony finds himself in hot water repeatedly after using his mastery of language to lie, cheat and steal his way through life. You won't love most of the choices he makes, but you'll continue to root for him and audiences will do so regardless of how well they know the actual Bourdain.

Tony star and director on not making Anthony Bourdain fans angry Tony is a new film loosely based on Anthony Bourdain's early years working at a Cape Cod seafood restaurant, starring Dominic Sessa.

That's the other tough thing about biopics: when it depicts a person that is so fresh in our collective memory (Bourdain was became world famous in the 2000s, and died in 2018), someone who had fans by the thousands and more than a few folks who had formed parasocial relationships with him (can any writer/foodie say they hadn't?), it needs to convince everyone to get on board with one director's idea of its subject. Johnson's take is nicely balanced between love for its star, and wisdom about the often dark subject matter.

Of course, artistic licence is taken with Bourdain's story here, but in choosing to show only one summer of his entire life, Johnson both limits himself creatively and gives himself room for interpretation. It's a smart move: even Bourdain himself would likely have trouble recalling that period of his life with intense accuracy; therefore, Johnson can build his base from Kitchen Confidential and experiment on top of it.

Michael Jibrin and Stavros Halkias put their co-worker through the wringer in Tony. (Supplied: A24)

The excellent supporting cast features Emilia Jones as Nancy, the woman who would later be Bourdain's first wife, Leo Woodall as loose-cannon line cook Sal, and Stavros Halkias as comic-relief Stavros. But it's Antonio Banderas as the head chef of the Flagship restaurant who truly shines.

World weary but never bereft of hope nor passion, Banderas's "Chef" is exactly the kind of mentor that Tony needs: a quiet, self-assured man who will let him sleep on the hammock rent-free, but will wake him up with a cold bucket of seawater every morning before showing him how to make sauce from scratch. He'll make you want to run away from your ordinary job and dive into the culinary arts as soon as possible.

Antonio Banderas took Dominic Sessa under his culinary wing both on and off-screen. (Supplied: A24)

Though Tony follows a somewhat predictable narrative structure, it has more than enough going for it to make the cinema trip worth it: specifically, its memorable central performance from Sessa, and what it says about endurance in the face of rejection, as well as following your passions to find where you belong.

Both Bourdain diehards and newcomers should walk away from this film feeling satiated.

Tony is in cinemas now.

World.title: Peter Garrett on the one thing more valuable than success
World.content:
Midnight Oil never made noise for the sake of it.

Politically driven and socially conscious, the legendary Australian rock band always made music with meaning, reflecting what they saw to be the greatest global and local injustices.

Watch every episode of Take 5 with Zan Rowe right here Catch interviews with Shania Twain, David Byrne, Darren Hayes, Jacinda Ardern and more.

Frontman Peter Garrett's first exposure to protest music came early.

In his episode of ABC TV's Take 5 with Zan Rowe, he recalls hearing African American spiritual turned civil rights anthem Tell It on the Mountain by American folk trio Peter, Paul and Mary as a child.

"When these first protest records started coming out, my mum went out and bought them and started playing them endlessly," he says. "So, I could hear this from my bedroom and then I got to know it and understand it."

The young Garrett was unaware it was a protest song. As with so much great art, his understanding of the song and its importance grew over the years.

"When I listened to it again, I was really transported not only to the memory of listening as a kid, but also what that song then became for people," he says.

"I had an awareness of now. It gave the song extra weight for me."

The making of a frontman

It wasn't long before a young Peter Garrett was putting his own voice out there.

"I started in choirs and I really loved it," he says. "I was one of the only boys in the church choir up on the North Shore in Sydney."

Upon starting university in Canberra, Garrett leapt at the chance to take the lead role in one of the rock bands on campus.

"I'm not shy," he says. "I'm lucky. I don't have stage fright or anything like that. So, I didn't have to be urged. I was ready to go.

"It was a band called Devil's Breakfast. Probably the worst name. That's what we sounded like. We changed our name, thankfully, to Rock Island Line."

Peter Garrett fronts Midnight Oil at a triple j concert at Sydney's Capitol Theatre in March 1982. (ABC)

That band was short-lived, but Garrett had the bug. After leaving Canberra, he wasted no time in joining up with a new set of musicians.

"Eventually I came up to Sydney and fell in with this other bunch of young miscreants. Rob Hirst, Jim Moginie, and later Martin Rotsey, and, yeah, the rest was history," he says.

The outfit, Midnight Oil, blew up Australia's booming pub rock scene in the late 1970s thanks to songs that were as intense, urgent and energetic as their breathless live shows. In the 80s and 90s, they became a global force, troubling charts in the UK, US, Canada and Europe.

Midnight Oil's alchemy is hard to explain: this doco is a good start The career-spanning documentary makes a strong attempt to convey what makes Midnight Oil one of the world's most powerful rock bands.

Hindsight may be 20/20, but Garrett swears he felt the magic from the outset.

"When I first came in to meet them, Rob started playing and so did Jim, they were 17 or 18, and I just looked at them and I went, 'Wow,'" he says.

"Something in me just knew that this was very special. I never knew how far it would go."

While Garrett has often seemed the face and figurehead of Midnight Oil, powerhouse drummer Rob Hirst, who died of cancer earlier this year, was another force behind many of their most enduring songs.

"Rob and I competed with one another sometimes," Garrett says. "It's like having a frontman on the drums, who's also a great singer and a songwriter," he says.

"Always with respect. Pushing to try and always make it as good as we could."

Protest music's continued relevance

Those drawn to Midnight Oil's music and message commonly lament the lack of protest music making waves in the current day.

Loading Instagram content

But music with a message is still out there. For Garrett, the missives of Filipino and Murrawarri artist Dobby ring loudly.

He chooses the song Dirrpi Yuin Patjulinya for his Take 5, a highlight from Dobby's ARIA-winning 2024 concept album Warrangu: River Story, which outlines the cultural importance of the Bogan, Culgoa and Barwon Rivers, and the over-irrigation and water theft that plagues them.

"I share the deep call from the heart that he has about the Murray-Darling, about what we've done to our river systems," Garrett says.

"I still don't think that we've gotten to the point with leaders, with governments, where we deeply understand how important the natural world is to us and what we're doing to it. He absolutely sums it up here. It is epic."

Any perceived dearth of protest music shouldn't be too surprising. In a precarious career environment for creatives, there are risks to sticking one's neck out. What's more, writing effective protest songs is difficult.

"Part of the challenge … is to try and have that work in a song where people don't run away from it whilst at the same time not being too self-conscious about it," Garrett says.

"[Dobby] has done it in a way which is very powerful and without reservation. It's epic in a way, and it's going right to the heart of where things are at now in country."

Hear extended episodes of Take 5 right here Dive even deeper into the music that has inspired your favourite artists on the Take 5 podcast.

It's not just a young man's game.

At 76, Bruce Springsteen also knows how to make protest music that connects.

Garrett considers the live version of the Edwin Starr classic War, recorded in Minneapolis around the time of this year's ICE raids, particularly electric.

"Tonight, we ask all of you to join with us in choosing hope over fear, democracy over authoritarianism," Springsteen rages in his intro.

"The rule of law over lawlessness, ethics over unbridled corruption, resistance over complacency, unity over division, and peace over war."

For Garrett, this call is a clear example of the impact of protest music.

"The way he introduces this song, and the way that they play it, says everything to me about what we all need to do in this era that we live in," Garrett says.

"The fact that he can get up and say, in a highly polarised country, this is what the times demand, he's really risen to the moment.

"It sounds as strong and as fresh and as needed as it was when he first played it, and when it was first written. Powerful. Necessary."

What drives us

Protest music is often born from rage and frustration. But the strongest examples aren't defeatist: they are driven by hope.

Double J — a place for music lovers Double J gives you the new music you'll actually love, alongside the classic tracks you keep coming back to. Give your playlist a rest and join us here.

"Hope is realising there can be a better future through action," Garrett says. "Hope is the antidote to apathy and disinterest and cynicism.

"So, hope becomes the most important and precious commodity that we have, but not hope which is born of wishful thinking, hope that's born of an understanding that it is people who change the world. It's people acting that make the difference."

And Garrett considers hope for the future a more appealing prospect than nostalgia. Despite spending most of his 73 years as a rock star or federal politician, Garrett isn't one to dwell.

"I don't look back," he says. "It's great to yarn about it, but I don't spend much time meditating on the past.

" At my stage of the game, my most precious resource by far, apart from love and family and connection, is time. There's nothing that's more important to me now than that. "

Even when performing on the stage of Sydney's Hordern Pavilion at this year's APRA Awards in tribute to Hirst, Garrett knew he had to get the job done, lest the gravity of the situation overwhelm him.

"The legacy of the band, in terms of my experience of it, it takes up so much space in how I think and feel," he says.

"If you start to get too introspective about it, or if you're always looking in the rear-vision mirror, or even assessing what it is, you're buggered."

At 73, Peter Garrett says time is one of his most precious resources. (ABC: Jess Gleeson)

Garrett's performance that night was not born from protest, but from celebration. But the approach remains the same no matter the task at hand.

"You've just got to be in the moment," he says.

"It's not easy to do, but it is the key. Hang in the moment, make the moment work as best as you can, and then out the door."

Watch every episode of Take 5 with Zan Rowe right now on ABC iview.

Hear extended interviews with all guests on the Take 5 podcast.

World.title: Keen to plant native flowers in your garden? We asked an expert for tips
World.content:
This National Science Week, we're celebrating all things native wildflowers.

But while they look gorgeous out in the wild, they can be a little tricky to grow in your garden — particularly if you're used to nurturing non-natives.

To try and help, we've compiled the best tips and tricks to try and make your wildflowers thrive.

Vote for Australia's most amazing wildflower These 10 flowers are not just pretty faces, they have superpowers. Which one will get your vote?

The most important rule, according to King's Park and Botanic Garden plant breeder Digby Growns, is to not expect all natives to be low maintenance or require the same things.

"It's horses for courses," he says.

"Some plants are more adaptable than others so try and start off with ones that are a bit tougher."

Can I grow any native plant?

Australia is a big place, and there are lots of different climates and environments, from deserts to rainforests, for plants to grow.

Mr Growns says that understanding where your plant is from and their needs helps avoid many beginner problems.

"If you're trying to grow West Australian plants, for instance, they generally need a really, really well-drained, almost sand-type soil," he says.

" So the number-one rule is to understand where your plants are from. "

Some species are versatile, growing across many regions.

Other plants exist in smaller areas and may struggle when moved to new climates.

But, there are ways to get beautiful plants from around the country, you just need to know what you're looking for.

Australian native kangaroo paws were originally found mostly in the south west of the country. (ABC Canberra: Jim Trail)

Kangaroo paws, for example, are native to southern Western Australia, but there are now cultivars bred to suit different conditions.

The original species — Anigozanthos flavidus — does best in its local area but hybrid cultivars can be grown widely and have more variation in flower colour, height, flower size, disease resilience and climate and soil adaptability.

How much upkeep is needed?

The amount of time you can spend gardening is a major factor when picking plants to grow.

Some Australian native plants, such as basket grass (Lomandra) and bottlebrushes (Callistemon) need little maintenance. While others, like native orchids for example, can require much more effort and know-how.

Take the time to choose the right plant, and you can save yourself time and money, according to Mr Growns.

He said that many botanical gardens, like King's Park have varieties of native species that are "pretty much bulletproof" and recommended as starter plants for gardeners who "struggle with a brown thumb".

For instance, Perth-based gardeners might like to try Ashby's banksia (Banksia ashbyi subsp. boreoscaia), grey cottonhead (Conostylis candicans) and the heart-leaf flame pea (Chorizema cordatum).

Do you need fire for native seeds?

Some of Australia's plants are activated only after a wildfire has gone through the area.

This is the case with some species of the flannel flower, one of the natives in this year's National Science Week poll to find the most amazing wildflower.

The flower blooms prolifically in the wild after bushfires, but to grow the plant yourself you don't need to light anything on fire.

"The seeds are recalcitrant and they require smoke water or aerosol smoke treatment to germinate," Mr Growns says.

"Kangaroo paws from seed need the same."

Importantly, the seeds you buy from a nursery will be pre-smoked, so they should grow without fire required.

Inside the heads of flannel flowers are a globe-like cluster of tiny flowers ringed by petal-like bracts. (ABC News: Emma Siossian)

You also don't necessarily need to grow natives from seed.

"There's quite a number of plants you can grow from cuttings," Mr Growns said.

"Some of the Calytrix [star flowers] you can, and small myrtaceous plants like melaleucas."

How often should I water natives?

While it will depend on the specific plant, there are a few tips and tricks that will work with a large number of natives.

Plant during mild weather months and, even if your chosen species is drought tolerant, it's recommended to water regularly until established.

This is because nursery plants are used to more water, so tapering them off stops the plants drying out.

Speaking of watering, it's a myth that Australian native plants don't need watering.

If you want a no-water native garden, choose plants that come from a similar rainfall and weather pattern as where you live.

Science quiz: Test your wildflower knowledge Just like our fauna, Australia's wildflowers are wildly unique and fascinating.

In a garden with a collection of Australian native plants with differing water requirements, supplementary irrigation is essential.

Use drip irrigation and do two to three deep soakings throughout the warmer weather.

Pruning is also a good idea for many natives.

For timing, the best rule of thumb is to trim immediately after a plant finishes flowering unless you want the seeds.

Remove up to a third of the growth, but don't cut down to bare wood where there's no leaves as this can result in a bare patch where nothing regrows.

Do I need different fertiliser?

If a plant is local to your area and soil type, the chances are it won't need a lot of interference or supplementary feeding.

But if you are looking at plants from across Australia keep in mind that they grow in different soils, climates and habitats so they all have different needs.

Some plants in the Proteaceae family, like banksias, grevilleas and hakeas, are quite sensitive to the amount of phosphorous found in general fertilisers.

These plants are very good at taking up existing phosphorous in the environment so a general fertiliser can be toxic.

There are plenty of low-phosphorous fertilisers that can be used instead for this group of plants and, if you want to keep things simple, you can use that same fertiliser on any other native plants in your garden too.

Potted plants are a different story, growing in isolation to the natural soil.

Top-dress containers of native plants every six months, using a slow-release fertiliser formulated for Australian plants.

Mr Growns says that no matter the native, your local nursery should be able to help get you started.

"Some nurseries like the big chain stores don't always have people that are fully across that [information on natives].

" But my recommendation is always go to a specialist nursery where you can. "

World.title: Trump says he will meet North Korea's Kim Jong Un later this year
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has announced he will meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un later this year, days after the United States scaled back military drills with South Korea.

"Yeah, I will be," Mr Trump said, when asked if he planned to meet Mr Kim later in 2026.

It would be the leaders first meeting during Mr Trump's second term.

Mr Trump specifically outlined Mr Kim's atomic arsenal while announcing his plans to meet with the leader.

Donald Trump met with the North Korean leader three times during his first term. (AP: Evan Vucci, File)

"I know Kim Jong Un very well, and he's going to be fine as long as we have a smart president," Mr Trump said.

"The fact that I get along with him — that's a good thing, not a bad thing."

" He has 57 very powerful nuclear weapons. "

In June, the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute estimated that North Korea had "possibly assembled around 60 warheads, possesses enough fissile material to produce at least 30 more".

Mr Trump and Mr Kim met three times during Mr Trump's first stint in the White House, with the US president saying they "fell in love" after exchanging "beautiful letters".

In recent days, Mr Trump has hinted at communication with Mr Kim, but he would not confirm whether the two had exchanged letters again recently.

Kim Jong Un's sister Kim Yo Jong said she was "unaware" of reported communication between her brother and Mr Trump, but said ties between the two were "excellent".

Kim Yo Jong described the ties between her brother, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, and Donald Trump as "excellent". (Korean Central News Agency/Korea News Service via AP, file)

It comes as Mr Trump ordered the Pentagon scale back planned joint military exercises with South Korea on Sunday, saying the exercises were costly and sent a "totally inappropriate and hostile" signal to North Korea.

He said in a social media post that North Korea had been "unthreatening and respectful" while he had been in the White House.

While Mr Trump did not give any further information about when he would meet Mr Kim, he is due to travel to China for an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in November.

South Korea has reduced its training drills with the United States from 11 days to five. (AP: Ahn Young-joon)

South Korea, US military drills to end early

South Korea and the United States reduced their annual joint military drills to five days from 11 and scaled back some field training after Mr Trump made the order.

Why Seoul has called for peace talks to formally end the Korean War South Korean President Lee Jae Myung has once again called for talks to formally end the Korean War which was only frozen and not ended by an armistice in 1953.

The change was announced on Wednesday as Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi began his visit to South Korea for regional security talks expected to cover developments on the Korean Peninsula.

South Korean president Lee Jae Myung said he recognised Mr Trump's "will and efforts to create conditions for dialogue" with North Korea.

"President Trump's message this time feels like a major decision made with careful consideration to create peace on the Korean Peninsula, moving beyond hostility and confrontation," he wrote on social media.

North Korea denounced the drills, calling the United States and South Korea "warmongers", and vowing to continue exercising its right to self-defence.

AFP/Reuters

World.title: New 'landmark' drug shown to prevent recurrence of deadly melanoma
World.content:
Two US pharmaceutical giants, Merck and Moderna, say an experimental melanoma drug that delivers treatment tailored to a patient's specific tumour prevented the deadly form of skin cancer from returning in a large clinical trial.

Called "intismeran autogene," it is based on the same messenger ribonucleic acid technology behind Covid-19 vaccines.

Researchers have been working on developing mRNA treatments against cancer, but this is the first time one has shown positive results in a Phase 3 trial.

When delivered along with pembrolizumab, an immunotherapy drug and the current standard of care, intismeran autogene prevented melanoma recurrence and prevented the cancer from spreading to other organs, the companies said in a statement.

The news sent shares in Moderna soaring 128 per cent to $US143 ($200) while Merck's stock was up more than 10 per cent to $US149.50.

The new drug is based off of a similar technology that Moderna and other pharmaceutical companies used for their Covid-19 vaccines. (Reuters: Dado Ruvic)

The trial lasted approximately a year and involved 1,137 patients who, following surgical removal of their cancers, were randomised into groups, with two-thirds receiving the new treatment plus pembrolizumab, while the rest received pembrolizumab alone.

The companies said they would present their data at an upcoming international conference and begin filings with regulators for approval.

Professor Georgina Long, the study's principal investigator and medical director of Melanoma Institute Australia said in a statement that the "results represent a landmark moment for adjuvant melanoma treatment".

How often should you be reapplying sunscreen? What three experts had to say about how to get the best protection from your sunscreen this summer.

"Intismeran in combination with pembrolizumab has the potential to establish a new treatment paradigm in the adjuvant melanoma setting, helping patients remain cancer-free for longer," she added.

The treatment works by taking a sample of the patient's tumour and identifying its unique mutational signature, or "fingerprint," then using messenger RNA technology to fight it.

Messenger RNA technology uses synthetic molecular instructions wrapped in tiny fat bubbles to teach the body how to make specific proteins.

The technology came to the fore during the Covid-19 pandemic, when Moderna and Pfizer developed vaccines that were highly effective against serious forms of the illness.

Melanoma is one of the deadliest forms of skin cancer, with more than 330,000 new cases diagnosed worldwide in 2022.

"Together with Merck, we are now studying intismeran in combination with pembrolizumab and other anti-cancer therapies, and as a monotherapy, across multiple tumour types and stages of disease, including melanoma, lung, bladder and kidney cancers," Moderna chief executive Stephane Bancel said in a statement.

AFP

World.title: $2 trillion of debt and climbing – Australia’s great big IOU is getting bigger
World.content:
PoliticsFederalGovernment debt $2 trillion of debt and climbing – Australia’s great big IOU is getting bigger Shane Wright August 20, 2026 — 4:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The nation’s governments will owe a combined $2 trillion by the end of the decade as the states and territories borrow at extraordinary rates that will force them to spend more of their budgets servicing their debts. Analysis released today by the independent Parliamentary Budget Office shows that in the case of Tasmania, interest repayments are on track to soar by more than 6000 per cent because of a blowout in debt levels while NSW and Victorian taxpayers face an increase of more than 400 per cent. The budget office, which has reviewed all state, territory and federal budgets, said deficits across them were all expected to narrow by the turn of the decade with small net operating surpluses in many cases. The federal government is the largest outlier with a deficit of $25.3 billion forecast for 2029-30. But government debt, particularly that carried by the states and territories, is growing sharply.



Related Article Opinion

Australian economy It’s my job to raise a topic neither side of politics will mention Ross Gittins Economics Editor According to the budget office, the states and territories had a combined $158.3 billion in gross debt in 2018-19. Federal gross debt was almost $650 billion. By the end of this decade, state and territory gross debt is forecast to reach a combined $770.9 billion – a 387 per cent increase. Federal government debt is expected to reach $1.2 trillion, a 92 per cent lift. Victoria faces the biggest debt load, forecast to reach $244.9 billion, an increase of 635 per cent. NSW’s debt is expected to climb by 440 per cent to $219.4 billion. But the largest increase is in Tasmania, where debt is on track to soar by 1850 per cent, from $600 million to $11.7 billion. Not only is debt expected to soar, but the state’s interest bill is forecast to explode by 6280 per cent from $10 million in 2018-19 to $638 million in 2029-30.



Before COVID, the federal government accounted for 80 per cent of all government debt. By 2029-30, the states and territories will account for almost 40 per cent of the expected $2 trillion in outstanding debt. Only the federal government and Western Australia are expected to keep their increase in gross debt to double figures over the period, although all parts of the country are facing a lift in the share of their revenue that goes to paying their interest bill. “The interest costs of paying off debt are forecast to take up a larger share of government revenue, rising from 4.1 per cent in 2024-25 to 6.2 per cent in 2028-29,” it said. While debt is climbing, the budget office said it was growing at a more gradual rate than expected in the round of budgets released last financial year. That was due to debt levels being a little better than forecast across most jurisdictions.



Federal gross debt alone was more than $20 billion lower than had been expected. The budget office said state and territory government spending is expected to climb steadily, going from a combined $263.5 billion ahead of the pandemic to $510 billion by the end of the decade. Cost overruns on large infrastructure projects, such as Melbourne’s Suburban Rail Loop, could hurt state government budgets. Joe Armao Over the same period, revenue is tipped to improve from $268.8 billion to almost $520 billion. “Forecast revenue has improved across jurisdictions, but these gains have generally been matched by higher forecast expenses,” it found.



According to the budget office, combined government debt is sustainable but each jurisdiction faces challenges. These include the risk of higher interest rates in part caused by the ongoing war in the Middle East and persistent inflation. Related Article Federal budget Australia retains AAA as tax changes and spending cuts help bottom line Infrastructure cost overruns, the chance of a property market correction which would eat into state and territory revenue forecasts and growing demand for services such as health and disability support could also weigh on budgets. The office also noted that volatility in federal and GST funding was a particular risk. The Productivity Commission last week released its interim report into the WA GST deal, which found it was a mistake that was on track to cost federal taxpayers almost $60 billion. At present, all states and territories are guaranteed by the federal government not to be left worse off by the deal.



That guarantee ends in 2030. Pressed on the commission’s report, which found the deal could lead to perverse outcomes such as WA getting a larger share of GST if there was a substantial bushfire in NSW, Treasurer Jim Chalmers stood by the current arrangement. “We’re not going to go through it page by page and respond to all of the detail in the interim report, except to say a fair go for WA is very, very important to us,” he said. World.title: Ex-bikie boss under investigation over alleged inducements to CFMEU officials
World.content:
Exclusive NationalVictoriaBuilding Bad Ex-bikie boss under investigation over alleged inducements to CFMEU officials Nick McKenzie August 20, 2026 — 4:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The former national vice-president of the Mongols outlaw bikie gang is being probed by police over allegations he offered inducements to officials still serving in the CFMEU in return for their support of his business. Ex-Mongol and former CFMEU delegate Tyrone “Little Ty” Bell is the target of a Taskforce Hawk operation examining whether CFMEU organisers leaked him information or co-ordinated union activity with him in order to advance the interests of Bell’s industrial relations consultancy. Tyrone Bell, a former Mongols bikie gang boss, now runs an industrial relations consultancy. The Hawk inquiry is significant for two reasons: it is the first “secret commissions” investigation undertaken by the state police taskforce combating wrongdoing in the building industry, and it is examining Bell’s dealings with serving rather than former CFMEU officials. It comes as Victoria Police expands its focus from investigating and prosecuting suspects to gathering information to supply the promised royal commission into the building industry.





Banking records reveal the same Comanchero figure received $690,000 in separate payments from a Big Build earthworks subcontractor working on the West Gate Tunnel project between May and October 2024. Both Carroll and Opposition Leader Jess Wilson have promised a Victorian royal commission, but neither has announced their preferred commissioner. Until an inquiry commences, Taskforce Hawk will remain as the lead entity tackling wrongdoing in the sector. Premier Ben Carroll promised a royal commission after taking over from Jacinta Allan last month. Eddie Jim Before its probe targeting Bell, Taskforce Hawk has focused on charging former union bosses and ex-CFMEU delegates, including those sacked in mid-July 2024 after this masthead kicked off its Building Bad series. Previous targets include ex-union officials who are alleged by Hawk to have engaged in bikie gang extortion activity in early 2026, many months after departing the union.



But the inquiry targeting Bell is focused on his relationship with at least two still-serving CFMEU organisers employed by the union while it remains under administration. Related Article Exclusive

Construction royal commission Allan’s wrong: Top crime fighters insist royal commission only solution Four sources with knowledge of the police activity, who would only speak on the basis that they were not identified, confirmed Hawk is probing allegations that these union officials secretly supported the ex-Mongol chief’s effort to win work advising major Victorian construction firms on industrial relations and safety matters. Victoria’s criminal code outlaws offering or providing any valuable benefit to a person without the knowledge of their employer – in this case the CFMEU administration. In a statement, Taskforce Hawk confirmed its “detectives are investigating after information was provided in relation to alleged secret commissions”.



“Warrants were executed in July and August this year at commercial properties in South Melbourne, Moorabbin, Melbourne and Richmond, as well as residential addresses in Wandin North, Seville, Yarra Junction and Officer South. No one has been arrested at this time,” the statement said. “As the investigation is active and ongoing, we are not in a position to provide further specific details.” Police are also probing how Bell obtained information about the CFMEU’s intention to target building companies as part of industrial activity in September 2025, and whether he used this inside information to sell the services of his industrial relations consulting business Dynamis. On Wednesday, Bell described the police allegations as “just ridiculous”. “I don’t really care because if there was something [I had done], I’d be in trouble then … I actually don’t know what they’re on about,” he told this masthead.



He dismissed claims that he had advance notice of union activity in late 2025 as the product of a “joke” he had shared with a building company owner who was considering engaging his firm. Bell also defended his close friendship with a still-serving CFMEU official, saying he had known the union organiser and his brother since primary school. The brother of the union organiser is a senior Hells Angels member. Tyrone Bell dismissed the police allegations on Wednesday. “I’ve been friends with him since primary school, and his brother and I feel very sorry for the guy because he loves his job,” Bell said of the CFMEU organiser. On Monday, the organiser told this masthead he had never taken any inducement from Bell or advised the ex-bikie about union activity. “I hope you don’t write anything bad about that guy because he’s a very good dad, a very good person,” Bell said of the unionist.



“We’ve all tried to not talk to him, and he’s a dear friend of mine. It’s very hard to do that.” Asked about the recent Hawk raids targeting him, Bell said: “If there is anything, go find it and charge the people. Go find it all then and charge them for whatever it is.” Bell also defended his relationship with major Victorian building company Markscon, saying he was previously paid to do “heaps of things” for the company. “I do heaps of running around and do stuff for them because they’re dear friends of mine, and they’ll pay me to do a service too. And I do lots of IR [industrial relations consulting] for them. There’s nothing wrong with that.”



Before becoming Markscon’s private IR adviser, Bell worked at the company as a CFMEU delegate. The owner of Markscon, Sam Marks, declined to answer questions when contacted on Wednesday. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: ‘I won’t be part of it’: Gambling ads in State of Origin an absurdity, says Liberal senator
World.content:
PoliticsFederalGambling ‘I won’t be part of it’: Gambling ads in State of Origin an absurdity, says Liberal senator Natassia Chrysanthos and Brittany Busch August 20, 2026 — 4:44am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

AFL and NRL audiences could still see an unlimited number of gambling ads during more than one-third of each season’s games, while the State of Origin series will continue to be mostly aired during time slots that have no ad limits under new wagering laws. Liberal Senator Paul Scarr cited the “absurdity” of those exemptions as he became the latest opposition MP vowing to vote against the contentious gambling package as the laws reach the Senate after months of debate. With the long-awaited gambling bill due to pass on Wednesday night, Rod Glover, the husband of late Labor MP Peta Murphy whose report three years ago catalysed a push for gambling ad bans, said the laws were a breakthrough “of sorts” but far from comprehensive. Online services say it will take years to sort out the opt-out register to block gambling ads. iStock Glover pointed the finger at the sports and media industries for lobbying the government to minimise any losses from gambling advertising revenue.



“The limits of the reforms reflect, in large part, the considerable lobbying power of the gambling industry, major sporting codes and media organisations,” Glover said on Wednesday. “Organisations with a privileged place in Australian life have continued to put their commercial interests in gambling ahead of the social responsibilities that come with the influence, standing and trust they hold.” The government’s new laws will limit gambling ads to three per hour for broadcast television and livestreaming services between 5am and 8.30pm. During those times, gambling ads can’t be shown during breaks, 15 minutes before the game or five minutes after. Without the Coalition amendments, the start time would have been 6am, the pre-game blackout would be five minutes, and streaming services would have been exempt from all those restrictions if they required their adult users to register, prove their age, and provide users an opt-out option. But either way, after 8.30pm, those rules don’t apply. The NRL and AFL both play multiple games each round where half-time breaks occur after 8.30pm.



Analysis by this masthead shows 75 of the 204 NRL games in the 2026 season will have been played with at least some of the half-time break after 8.30pm in NSW and Victoria. For the AFL, 86 games out of 207 across the season continue to be broadcast past 8.30pm. This masthead confirmed sports betting ads were seen during these game breaks last weekend. Related Article Analysis

Gambling Labor, Coalition agree gambling can police itself. Good luck with that The State of Origin’s three annual games – often the most viewed television events each year – all begin after 8pm, meaning unlimited gambling ads can be shown at half-time. The women’s competition also has half-time breaks that fall after 8.30pm. Scarr described the package as “such a flawed piece of legislation that I have no choice but to cross the floor”. “How many kids are going to be watching State of Origin from 8.05 to 8.30 and then go to bed at 8.30, and after 8.30 it becomes open slather? It’s an absurdity and I won’t be part of it,” he said.



Labor this week secured the Coalition’s support to pass its gambling laws by agreeing to a series of last-minute amendments to strengthen the legislation. While the compromise continued to disappoint crossbenchers, harm reduction advocates, former gambling addicts and their families – who wanted a full ban on gambling ads and inducements – Labor and the Coalition say they have struck the right balance. Industry scratches head over last-minute changes But the government now has a raft of complicated last-minute changes it needs to deal with. A key one relates to the new “AdStop” regime that will give Australians a one-stop shop for opting out of gambling ads across their online accounts. This was another push from the Coalition, concerned it would be too cumbersome for people to opt out of platforms individually.



The scheme will be administered by the Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA), using funding from a levy to be imposed on gambling companies. It could involve people nominating either their email address or mobile phone number to the ACMA register. Related Article Gambling ‘I can’t stop to save my own life’: Parents read son’s final plea on gambling addiction While media companies were broadly happy with the amendments – given they will now be able to adhere to broadcast rules rather than set-up age verification and opt-out tools – tech companies did not know how the new scheme would work. The industry thinks matching emails across all platforms will be difficult given people have multiple addresses, while there were privacy concerns about how data would be securely shared between the ACMA register and a multitude of online platforms. There were also questions about how the system would communicate real-time updates, including how platforms would receive the data.



Government sources also conceded the technical work would be complex and take time to work through, meaning the scheme would not be ready by the time the new ad laws come into force in January. BetStop, the exclusion register, took years to finalise. Independent Senator David Pocock said the legislation failed on many levels. “We have four out of five Australians wanting a ban on all gambling ads, and yet the government is trying to sell us this [as] getting the balance right, which is three ads per hour on TV and a fairly unworkable opt-out system online,” he said. World.title: No criminal probe over Israeli strike that killed Australian Zomi Frankcom
World.content:
Israel’s military has cleared its personnel of any criminal wrongdoing over an attack in Gaza that killed seven aid workers including Australian Zomi Frankcom. The Israeli Defence Forces (IDF) decided there was “no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct” in the strike on the World Central Kitchen (WCK) workers in April 2024 as they delivered humanitarian aid to a warehouse. Australian Zomi Frankcom was killed in a 2024 airstrike while delivering aid in Gaza with World Central Kitchen. The formal IDF decision came hours after Foreign Minister Penny Wong called for “full accountability” over the deaths, as she honoured Frankcom at an event in Canberra on Wednesday to launch a humanitarian award in her name. The outcome was one of five IDF reports issued on Wednesday into separate incidents. In one case, which made global headlines, five-year-old Palestinian girl Hind Rajab died in January 2024 after pleading to be rescued from an attack that had killed her aunt, uncle and three cousins.



The IDF ruled there should be a criminal investigation by the Military Police into the death of Rajab, her family members, as well as paramedics who sought to come to her aid. Hind Rajab, who was killed alongside her family in an Israeli strike in 2024. Family Handout via AP In a second case, the IDF decided there should also be a criminal investigation into an ambush by Israeli forces that killed 15 Palestinians including medical personnel as well as a United Nations employee in March 2025. The decision on Frankcom and her colleagues outraged WCK, which condemned the outcome and called for an independent inquiry into the airstrikes on the grounds that the Israeli military could not credibly investigate its own conduct. Frankcom, 43, and six colleagues died on April 1, 2024 when the vehicle they were travelling in was fired upon while delivering aid in Gaza.



The IDF said its officers had “mistakenly believed that the vehicles contained Hamas military operatives and therefore struck the vehicles”. It claimed that attempts were made to contact WCK representatives during “the approximately half-hour period in which the convoy vehicles were tracked on the understanding that they contained Hamas operatives”, but those attempts were unsuccessful. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict ‘We have expressed sympathy’: Israeli ambassador declines to apologise for Zomi Frankcom killing The Israeli military said the presence of armed security to accompany the convoy “was not coordinated with IDF authorities” and the vehicles had deviated from the route arranged in advance, while several people were also mistakenly identified as armed persons. “Following review of all findings of the factual assessment, it was determined that, notwithstanding serious failures in the process that led to the assessment that Hamas operatives were travelling in the vehicles, the decisions of the commanders did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct,” the IDF said.



It added that there was “no reasonable suspicion of criminal misconduct that would justify the opening of a criminal investigation”. Two Israeli officers were dismissed from their positions and three senior officers were formally reprimanded, according to the Israeli military. WCK said it fundamentally disagreed with the decision not to pursue a criminal investigation. “We strongly condemn the Israeli military prosecutor’s account of the deaths of our seven colleagues on April 1, 2024,” the aid organisation said in a statement. “There has never been any excuse or justification for the attacks, and there is nothing in this account that does so. The decision is inconsistent with the full truth and deeply offensive.”



Wong spoke in Canberra on Wednesday at a Parliament House event attended by Frankcom’s family to launch the Zomi Frankcom Humanitarian Award. “Two years on from Zomi Frankcom’s death, the pain of her loss remains with us,” she said. “People like Zomi are rare, and their courage deserves to be celebrated. “I want to make it clear that the Australian government continues to press the Israeli government for full accountability for the deaths of Zomi and her World Central Kitchen colleagues. Zomi and her family deserve justice.” Foreign Affairs Minister Penny Wong with Zomi Frankcom’s brother Mal Frankcom, pictured in September 2025. Dominic Lorrimer



In a report released in July 2024, former Australian Defence Force chief Mark Binskin found that “a significant breakdown in situational awareness” by the Israeli military caused the strike that killed Frankcom, adding he did not believe the charity workers were deliberately targeted. The IDF said its Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism (FFAM) had reviewed approximately 150 incidents since the beginning of the war, then transferred them for examination by the Military Prosecution. Rajab and her family were trapped in a vehicle under fire in Gaza City in January 2024, while she pleaded for help by phone with her cousin Layan Hamada beside her. The IDF concluded that in the hours shortly after the firing, following a telephone call to rescue authorities, the movement of a Palestine Red Crescent ambulance was coordinated for the purpose of evacuating the casualties. “However, according to the allegations raised, upon the ambulance’s arrival at the scene of the incident, a shell was fired toward it, resulting in the deaths of the two paramedics travelling in it,” the IDF said.



Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Netanyahu bluntly rejects Trump’s Gaza plan to disarm Hamas “Several days later, the bodies of the seven members of the Hamada family, including the bodies of Hind and Layan, were recovered from the vehicle. In addition, the bodies of the two paramedics were recovered from the ambulance. “It has been decided to initiate a criminal investigation of the incident by Military Police Criminal Investigation Division (MPCID). In light of this decision, no further details can be provided beyond the above with respect to the aspects arising from the FFAM’s review.” The 15 Palestinian paramedics were killed as they drove in the southern city of Rafah in March 2025. The IDF decided not to take criminal action over the killings of four staffers from Doctors Without Borders in two separate instances in November 2023 and February 2024.



On Wednesday, an Israeli airstrike killed nine Palestinians at a police station in Gaza, medics said. Medics and police sources said several officers were among those killed at what the Hamas-led interior ministry said was the headquarters of the municipal police. Fifteen others were wounded. The Israeli military said it had struck Hamas militants who “operated from the civilian police station” to advance attacks against its troops. with Reuters Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Judge finds King Eddies negligent after catastrophic birth-injury but rules against compensation payout
World.content:
NationalWACourts Judge finds King Eddies negligent after catastrophic birth-injury but rules against compensation payout Rebecca Peppiatt August 20, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Perth family has lost a catastrophic birth-injury lawsuit against a major maternity hospital despite a judge finding clinicians were negligent, after a court ruled their daughter’s severe brain damage was legally “inevitable.” The girl, whom WAtoday has chosen not to name, was born in August 2020 at 38-weeks gestation due to issues picked up during a routine examination at King Edward Memorial Hospital in Subiaco. King Edward Memorial Hospital. An ultrasound had shown growth restriction, reduced amniotic fluid and abnormal cerebral blood flow that pointed to the unborn baby being in distress and doctors advised the parents she should be delivered early. How the baby would be born was then discussed with hospital staff, and a dispute over whether the parents were offered an induced natural labour or an elective caesarean began.



The parents later told the Supreme Court of WA that they were told an elective caesarean was “not an option in a public hospital”. However, the court preferred the evidence of the doctors, finding that an elective caesarean was available but the parents declined it by choice. Court documents showed the mother held a strong preference for a vaginal birth so was later induced, but monitoring of the baby’s heart rate showed she was in distress and needed to be delivered urgently with an emergency caesarean. Doctors stated that the father spent the next 20 to 30 minutes asking questions about the risks of the surgery. The baby’s distressed state continued, with medical notes showing her heart rate was deteriorating and her delivery became a category-1 emergency.



Despite the extreme urgency, the father continued questioning the doctors for another five to 10 minutes, the documents claimed. The mother then gave oral consent, but only after a physical examination confirmed her cervix was not sufficiently dilated and a vaginal birth was no longer possible. As she was being wheeled into the operating theatre after signing the consent form, doctors told the court that the father kept the form, edited it and crossed out two deletions of standard clauses that included consent for clinical photographs and vaginal examinations by supervised medical students under anaesthesia. Surgical staff were then under pressure to find the consent form without knowing the father still had it, with allegations that the surgeon declared he had to go ahead without the form because it was an emergency. Doctors told the court that this delayed carrying out the caesarean, but the father disputed the evidence and said he handed it over the first time it was asked.



The delay in obtaining consent proved fatal to the family’s legal case. Related Article Courts WA couple win Supreme Court battle to become same-sex parents through surrogacy The family argued that the hospital was negligent in failing to recognise the earlier need for a caesarean. However, the judge ruled that because a doctor cannot legally perform surgery without consent, and because the parents’ pattern of questioning took approximately 30 minutes to resolve, recommending a caesarean earlier would not have resulted in an earlier delivery. The court concluded that the mother would not have consented any earlier than she did, meaning the baby’s injuries were legally “inevitable” and not caused by the hospital’s prior negligence.



Despite this, the judge still ruled that the hospital was legally negligent because it breached its duty of care when a midwife paged the registrar to review a highly concerning heart trace. The court found that the doctor did not review the CTG history, did not speak to the midwife, and did not ask why she had been paged. Instead, she did no more than “glance” at the screen and left the room. The judge ruled that this complete failure to undertake an interpretation of the CTG fell short of the precautions a reasonable hospital would have taken to mitigate the risk of oxygen deprivation. However, the claim was dismissed because the judge ultimately found the baby’s hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury was unavoidable and not caused by the hospital’s actions.



The little girl, now five years- old, survived a prolonged resuscitation but was left with grade-three brain damage, cerebral palsy, functional blindness, and impaired hearing. Her parents pursued legal action in order to secure financial compensation to help support their daughter, who has ongoing impairments likely to persist for the rest of her life. The judge closed his remarks by acknowledging his findings would be “of little consolation” to a family left wondering how their daughter suffered profound injuries while in the hospital’s care. A GoFundMe page has raised almost $7000 of a $55,000 target for the girl to have “breakthrough treatment” overseas to stimulate her brain and potentially offer improvements in her quality of life. Her father wrote that she “continues to show strength, awareness and joy”, adding that “her resilience is beyond words”.

World.title: Matt Comyn offloads $8.4m of CBA shares amid separation from wife
World.content:
NationalCBD Opinion Matt Comyn offloads $8.4m of CBA shares amid separation from wife John Buckley CBD columnist August 19, 2026 — 9:20pm

August 19, 2026 — 9:20pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Executives sell shares in their own companies all the time. So when Commonwealth Bank chief executive Matt Comyn offloaded about $8.4 million worth of shares last week, we didn’t think much of it. But that was before we knew Comyn and his wife, Lucy, are working through the terms of their separation, which CBD brought word of on Tuesday, after the Commonwealth Bank confirmed the couple had split. Commonwealth Bank chief Matt Comyn presents the bank’s full year 2026 results. Nic Long The share disclosure, released to the market on August 14, showed Comyn acquired a tick over 30,000 shares as a result of vested equity earned as part of his remuneration. Then there were two tranches of shares sold: The first tranche of 30,006 shares sold at $168.18 per share, worth a little over $5 million. The second lot of 20,091 shares went at $168.80, worth about $3.4 million. All up, the share movement leaves Comyn’s direct shareholding about the same as it was the day before, and is not out of step with his previous share sales, which have occurred at least once a year since 2022. A Commonwealth Bank spokesman declined to comment on whether Comyn’s share sale this month was related to his separation.



But our guess is the sale, the second tranche of which was jointly held by Comyn and his wife as beneficiaries of a trust, freed up a helpful chunk of cash for whatever costs are racked up through the separation, and, of course, may make it easier for the couple to split their assets. Another Pauline whisperer It was only June when we last brought word of the frenzy among corporates to find so-called “Pauline whisperers” to cosy up to One Nation as the party rises in the polls. Well, it looks like business is good enough for those who already have a line into One Nation leader Pauline Hanson to flaunt their access. One lobbyist who has since made the pitch for those betting that Hanson’s popularity will hold out until at least 2028 is Jannette Cotterell, who set up her lobby shop Executive Counsel Australia back in 2008 following a five-year stint at CT Group, formerly known as Crosby Textor.



Cotterell describes herself as non-partisan, and in a post to LinkedIn felt it necessary to declare “engagement does not equal endorsement”. We bet! When reached on Tuesday, Cotterell was quick to have a crack at us over the sausagefest of names that populated our last column item on the matter. She was also quick to take the opportunity to pump up her own tyres. But we’ll spare you the marketing material. Cotterral’s name joins a string of others who have been bandied about in political circles as possible One Nation relationship brokers. So far we’ve heard the name of Gina Rinehart’s media minder James Radford come up. So too former Nationals deputy campaign director and conservative lobbyist Michael Kauter. Also: Scott Mitchell, who spent five years as the federal director of the Nationals before setting up his own lobby shop. We’re sure they’re freshening up their pitch decks. Life after Ley Former opposition leader Sussan Ley’s ex-spinner Liam Jones may be having a little trouble letting go of his old life, as CBD brought word of last week.



But it looks like Ley’s former chief of staff Dean Shachar has had no such trouble moving on – to a meeting with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, no less. On Wednesday, Shachar was quick to brag about his rendezvous with Albanese in Canberra in a post to LinkedIn, after the PM was able to squeeze in some time in the diary to hear all about Shachar’s new employer, the retail share trading platform, Superhero. But apparently it wasn’t just Albo and Shachar there to chew the fat. Also present were the company’s co-founders, chief executive John Winters and chief technology officer Wayne Baskin, who presented Albo with a Hawthorn Football Club jersey. The Superhero founders were simply flogging their own wares, given the company is a back-of-jersey sponsor. But who knows, given Albo’s approach to politics, the Hawks may be in with a shot to win over a new supporter. The PM wasn’t the only one who had to sit through the pitch. Winters and Shachar were also seen at Aussies on Thursday morning in talks with Chris Taylor, the newly minted chief of staff to One Nation leader Pauline Hanson. The Superhero guys also made overtures to Opposition Leader Angus Taylor’s office on Wednesday, CBD hears, and met with several Coalition MPs through the week.



Airwallex Cafe It would seem no idea is too corny for the Airwallex marketing team. There was the financial start-up’s bizarre co-sponsorship of a function on a yacht called “Mischief”. Then the company’s sponsorship of Essendon Football Club. Now the company has set up a pop-up cafe. But our guess is any idea that distracts from the audit announced by the nation’s financial crimes agency AUSTRAC this year is probably considered a good one. “Yeah, I mean look, it’s just a great opportunity where we know people are in town candidly, and like the majority of people here are customers,” the company’s Australia and New Zealand boss James Teodorini said on Wednesday. “We’re lucky – I was just speaking to someone who’s been a customer for nine years and they were like, want to come down and say hi. “Um, it’s an opportunity while people are in town. Not to go and necessarily do this versus that, but just talk about who we are.” Nice one.



The cafe was set up around the corner from the ICC in Sydney, where Airwallex’s rival payments company, Stripe, was hosting an event of its own. As far as stunts go, this has to be among the lamest. World.title: $2 trillion of debt and climbing – Australia’s great big IOU is getting bigger
World.content:
PoliticsFederalGovernment debt $2 trillion of debt and climbing – Australia’s great big IOU is getting bigger Shane Wright August 20, 2026 — 4:55am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The nation’s governments will owe a combined $2 trillion by the end of the decade as the states and territories borrow at extraordinary rates that will force them to spend more of their budgets servicing their debts. Analysis released today by the independent Parliamentary Budget Office shows that in the case of Tasmania, interest repayments are on track to soar by more than 6000 per cent because of a blowout in debt levels while NSW and Victorian taxpayers face an increase of more than 400 per cent. The budget office, which has reviewed all state, territory and federal budgets, said deficits across them were all expected to narrow by the turn of the decade with small net operating surpluses in many cases. The federal government is the largest outlier with a deficit of $25.3 billion forecast for 2029-30. But government debt, particularly that carried by the states and territories, is growing sharply.



Related Article Opinion

Australian economy It’s my job to raise a topic neither side of politics will mention Ross Gittins Economics Editor According to the budget office, the states and territories had a combined $158.3 billion in gross debt in 2018-19. Federal gross debt was almost $650 billion. By the end of this decade, state and territory gross debt is forecast to reach a combined $770.9 billion – a 387 per cent increase. Federal government debt is expected to reach $1.2 trillion, a 92 per cent lift. Victoria faces the biggest debt load, forecast to reach $244.9 billion, an increase of 635 per cent. NSW’s debt is expected to climb by 440 per cent to $219.4 billion. But the largest increase is in Tasmania, where debt is on track to soar by 1850 per cent, from $600 million to $11.7 billion. Not only is debt expected to soar, but the state’s interest bill is forecast to explode by 6280 per cent from $10 million in 2018-19 to $638 million in 2029-30.



Before COVID, the federal government accounted for 80 per cent of all government debt. By 2029-30, the states and territories will account for almost 40 per cent of the expected $2 trillion in outstanding debt. Only the federal government and Western Australia are expected to keep their increase in gross debt to double figures over the period, although all parts of the country are facing a lift in the share of their revenue that goes to paying their interest bill. “The interest costs of paying off debt are forecast to take up a larger share of government revenue, rising from 4.1 per cent in 2024-25 to 6.2 per cent in 2028-29,” it said. While debt is climbing, the budget office said it was growing at a more gradual rate than expected in the round of budgets released last financial year. That was due to debt levels being a little better than forecast across most jurisdictions.



Federal gross debt alone was more than $20 billion lower than had been expected. The budget office said state and territory government spending is expected to climb steadily, going from a combined $263.5 billion ahead of the pandemic to $510 billion by the end of the decade. Cost overruns on large infrastructure projects, such as Melbourne’s Suburban Rail Loop, could hurt state government budgets. Joe Armao Over the same period, revenue is tipped to improve from $268.8 billion to almost $520 billion. “Forecast revenue has improved across jurisdictions, but these gains have generally been matched by higher forecast expenses,” it found.



According to the budget office, combined government debt is sustainable but each jurisdiction faces challenges. These include the risk of higher interest rates in part caused by the ongoing war in the Middle East and persistent inflation. Related Article Federal budget Australia retains AAA as tax changes and spending cuts help bottom line Infrastructure cost overruns, the chance of a property market correction which would eat into state and territory revenue forecasts and growing demand for services such as health and disability support could also weigh on budgets. The office also noted that volatility in federal and GST funding was a particular risk. The Productivity Commission last week released its interim report into the WA GST deal, which found it was a mistake that was on track to cost federal taxpayers almost $60 billion. At present, all states and territories are guaranteed by the federal government not to be left worse off by the deal.



That guarantee ends in 2030. Pressed on the commission’s report, which found the deal could lead to perverse outcomes such as WA getting a larger share of GST if there was a substantial bushfire in NSW, Treasurer Jim Chalmers stood by the current arrangement. “We’re not going to go through it page by page and respond to all of the detail in the interim report, except to say a fair go for WA is very, very important to us,” he said.
